assets.domain: Social Neuroscience | Prejudice | In-group/Out-group | Contact Hypothesis
assets.topic: From Them to Us: Is Prejudice Inevitable, or Can We Expand Our Circle of Concern?
assets.subject_baseline: A common view, supported by evolutionary psychology, is that prejudice is inevitable. Our brains evolved to favor in-group members and be wary of out-group members. This 'tribal instinct' kept our ancestors alive. The claim is that prejudice is a natural, hardwired feature of human cognition that can be managed but never truly overcome. Goleman challenges this, arguing that the same neural plasticity that creates prejudice can also overcome it.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Researcher: 'You're saying prejudice is not inevitable? But every human society has in-group bias. Newborns prefer faces of their own race. The amygdala responds with fear to out-group faces within milliseconds. This is hardwired.' Subject: 'Newborn preferences are about familiarity, not prejudice. The amygdala's response to out-group faces is eliminated when the person has extensive positive contact with that group. The contact hypothesis is one of the most robust findings in social psychology: under the right conditions — equal status, common goals, intergroup cooperation, and institutional support — contact reduces prejudice. The key mechanism: when we get to know an out-group member as an individual, the brain re-categorizes them from 'them' to 'us.' The orbitofrontal cortex assigns hedonic value based on experience. Repeated positive contact with out-group members can retrain this valuation system.' Researcher: 'But what about deep-seated prejudice that's been reinforced for years?' Subject: 'Goleman's argument is that the same neural plasticity that allows prejudice to form also allows it to be unlearned. The neural scaffolding of prejudice is built through repeated associations. It can be dismantled through counter-stereotypical experiences, perspective-taking, and — most importantly — personal relationships that cross group boundaries. The 'from them to us' shift is not just conceptual — it's neural. When someone becomes 'us,' they activate the same brain circuits as self and family. The practical implication: contact works. Integration works. The solution to prejudice is not to suppress our tribal instincts but to expand the definition of 'us.'
observed_nonverbal_log: Newborns prefer faces of own race — but this is familiarity, not prejudice; it disappears with exposure to diverse faces
Amygdala response to out-group faces: fear response within milliseconds — BUT eliminated with extensive positive contact
Contact hypothesis (Gordon Allport): equal status, common goals, cooperation, institutional support — these conditions reliably reduce prejudice
The 'minimal group paradigm' (Tajfel): even arbitrary group assignments (Klee vs Kandinsky) produce in-group favoritism
Neural re-categorization: when out-group members become known individuals, the brain shifts them from 'them' to 'us' category
assets.question: Goleman challenges the claim that prejudice is inevitable and cannot be overcome. He argues that the same neural mechanisms that create prejudice can also reduce it. What is the evidence for this claim, and what conditions must be met for prejudice reduction to occur?
assets.correct_diagnosis: The evidence: (1) The contact hypothesis (Gordon Allport, 1954) — under conditions of equal status, common goals, intergroup cooperation, and institutional support, contact reduces prejudice. This is one of the most replicated findings in social psychology. (2) Neural plasticity — the orbitofrontal cortex assigns hedonic value based on experience. Positive contact with out-group members retrains this system. The amygdala's fear response to out-group faces is eliminated with extensive positive contact. (3) Re-categorization — when we get to know an out-group member as a person, the brain shifts them from 'them' to 'us.' This activates self-related brain circuits for that person. The implication: the 'us' category is not fixed. It can expand. (4) Minimal group paradigm (Tajfel) — even arbitrary group assignments (preference for Klee vs Kandinsky paintings) produce in-group favoritism. This shows both how easily 'us/them' distinctions form AND how arbitrary they are. If they can be created arbitrarily, they can be overcome. (5) Conditions that work: cooperative learning (jigsaw classroom where each student has a piece of the puzzle), cross-group friendships (the strongest predictor of reduced prejudice), and superordinate goals (goals that require cooperation across groups). The limits: contact alone is not enough — it must meet Allport's conditions. Superficial contact can reinforce stereotypes. But genuine, equal-status, cooperative contact across group boundaries reliably reduces prejudice. The brain's capacity to expand the circle of 'us' is the neural basis of hope for reducing tribalism.
distractors: Contact alone is sufficient to reduce prejudice — any interaction between groups will automatically improve relations
Prejudice is entirely a product of culture and socialization — biology plays no role in how we form in-group/out-group distinctions
The minimal group paradigm shows that prejudice is created by competition for resources — without competition, there is no prejudice
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Stage 1 — Automatic categorization: The brain automatically categorizes people as in-group or out-group based on salient features (race, age, gender, language). This is fast and automatic (low road). Stage 2 — Evaluative tagging: The OFC assigns hedonic value based on prior experience and cultural learning. Negative associations trigger amygdala alarm. Stage 3 — Contact opportunity: When the right conditions are met (equal status, common goals, cooperation, institutional support), positive contact provides new data that contradicts the negative associations. Stage 4 — Re-categorization: Repeated positive contact retrains the OFC and quiets the amygdala. The individual is re-categorized from 'them' to 'us.' The practical implication: prejudice is not destiny. The brain can learn to expand its circle of concern. But this requires intentional contact, not mere coexistence.

assets.visual_frame_description: A laboratory file room where case cards stream past a reaction-time scanner counting in tenths of seconds, while a wall of portraits - Bill Cosby, Martin Luther King, Jr., Jeffrey Dahmer, Marie Curie - flickers above the cabinets.
key_concepts: During the last years of apartheid in South Africa, thirty people - half white business executives, half black community organizers - met clandestinely for four days to be trained to conduct leadership seminars together

On the last day the group sat riveted to a television while President F. W. de Klerk gave the now-famous speech that legalized banned organizations and ordered the release of many political prisoners, as Anne Inersebe pictured the face of someone she knew for each organization named

In the ending ritual, a tall, emotionally reserved Afrikaaner stood, looked directly at Anne Inersebe, and said, 'I want you to know that I was raised to think you were an animal' - and with that he broke into tears

As Walter Kaufmann, the translator of Martin Buber, put it, with 'Us-Them' the world is divided in two: the children of light and the children of darkness, the sheep and the goats, the elect and the damned

The relationship between one of Us and one of Them by definition lacks empathy, let alone attunement - the gulf builds with the silencing of empathy, and across that gulf we are free to project onto Them whatever we like

In experiments where volunteers were asked if they would take an electrical shock in place of someone they could not see, the more unlike themselves the other person was described as being, the more unwilling they were to come to the rescue
'Hatred,' said Elie Wiesel, the Nobel Peace Prize winner and Holocaust survivor, 'is a cancer that is passed from one person to another, one people to another'
Northern Irish Protestants and Catholics, like Serbs and Croatians, have battled over the years though genetically they are each other's closest biological brothers and sisters
Groups that are so much alike move from Us to Them via the 'narcissism of minor differences,' seizing on small features that set the groups apart while ignoring their vast human similarities
Prejudice is a hypothesis desperately trying to prove itself to us: once a negative bias begins, we seize on whatever seems to confirm the bias and ignore what does not

Outright anger primes prejudice even in those whose biases are slight - like a match on tinder, antagonism catalyzes the switch from Us and Them, the mere perception of difference, to Us versus Them, active hostility

When flooded by anger and fear, both amygdala-driven, the prefrontal area becomes incapacitated as the low road hijacks the high, sabotaging the ability to think clearly about whether he really has all the bad traits we ascribe to Them

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Interpersonal Radar Sweep
assets.visual_frame_description: A command post bathed in blue light where a wall of monitors plays split-second social moments; over each frame a radar sweep draws a red ring around the telling detail while a gauge labeled Wired to Connect swings between Linkup and Corrosion.
assets.player_mission: Scan a grid of freeze-frames from the book's opening scenes and name the neural or social signature in each: the crowd's mood morphing under Lieutenant Colonel Christopher Hughes's orders, the spindle-cell snap decision, the dopamine flash at a direct gaze, the kindergarten tantrum in Fort Worth, the German motorcyclist ignored for fifteen minutes. Judge whether each moment belongs to the wired-to-connect brain or to social corrosion before the scanner stamps its verdict.
key_concepts: During the early days of the second American invasion of Iraq, soldiers set out for a local mosque to contact the town's chief cleric, but a mob of hundreds of devout Muslims surrounded the heavily armed platoon, waving their hands in the air and shouting, fearing the soldiers were coming to arrest their spiritual leader or destroy the mosque, a holy shrine

Lieutenant Colonel Christopher Hughes picked up a loudspeaker and told his soldiers to 'take a knee,' meaning to kneel on one knee, then ordered them to point their rifles toward the ground, and finally gave the order 'Smile' - at that the crowd's mood morphed, most smiling in return and patting the soldiers on the back as they walked slowly away, backward, still smiling

The most fundamental revelation of this new discipline is that 'we are wired to connect' - neuroscience has discovered that our brain's very design makes it sociable, inexorably drawn into an intimate brain-to-brain linkup whenever we engage with another person

Our social interactions operate as modulators, something like interpersonal thermostats that continually reset key aspects of our brain function as they orchestrate our emotions, sending out cascades of hormones that regulate biological systems from our heart to our immune cells

The brain-to-brain link allows our strongest relationships to shape us on matters as benign as whether we laugh at the same jokes or as profound as which genes are or are not activated in T-cells, the immune system's foot soldiers in the constant battle against invading bacteria and viruses
That link is a double-edged sword: nourishing relationships have a beneficial impact on our health, while toxic ones can act like slow poison in our bodies

Emotional Intelligence, published in 1995, focused on managing our own emotions - a one-person psychology - while this book is a companion volume that enlarges the picture to a two-person psychology, what transpires as we connect

Spindle cells, a newly discovered class of neuron, act the most rapidly of any, guiding snap social decisions for us - and have proven to be more plentiful in the human brain than in any other species
Mirror neurons, a different variety of brain cells, sense both the move another person is about to make and their feelings, and instantly prepare us to imitate that movement and feel with them
When the eyes of a woman that a man finds attractive look directly at him, his brain secretes the pleasure-inducing chemical dopamine - but not when she looks elsewhere

The social brain is the only biological system in our bodies that continually attunes us to, and in turn becomes influenced by, the internal state of people we're with; all other biological systems mainly regulate their activity in response to signals emerging from within the body, not beyond our skin

Through 'neuroplasticity,' repeated experiences sculpt the shape, size, and number of neurons and their synaptic connections, so being chronically hurt and angered, or being emotionally nourished, by someone we spend time with daily over the course of years can gradually refashion our brain

assets.topic: Dialogue: The Loudspeaker at the Mosque
assets.visual_frame_description: A dust-choked street before a mosque in Iraq; a heavily armed platoon kneels in a semicircle, rifles pointed at the ground, while a loudspeaker crackles with one word - 'Smile' - and the crowd's shouting wavers into returned smiles.
assets.player_mission: Play Lieutenant Colonel Christopher Hughes on the mosque road in Iraq: read the level of hostility in that crowd, sense what would calm them, bet on the discipline of your men and their trust in you, and gamble on hitting just the right gesture that pierces the barriers of language and culture. Then switch seats and play the mob as the platoon kneels and smiles - decide whether the spell holds before anyone raises a rifle.
key_concepts: Hughes's quick-witted move was the culmination of a dizzying array of split-second social calculations: reading the level of hostility in that crowd and sensing what would calm them, betting on the discipline of his men and the strength of their trust in him, and gambling on hitting just the right gesture that would pierce the barriers of language and culture
That well-calibrated forcefulness, combined with adeptness at reading people, distinguishes outstanding law enforcement officers - and certainly military officers dealing with agitated civilians
Whatever one's feelings about the military campaign itself, that incident spotlights the brain's social brilliance even in a chaotic, tense encounter

The same neural circuits Hughes relied on are the ones we use when we encounter a potentially sinister stranger and decide instantly whether to run or engage - this interpersonal radar has saved countless people over human history and remains crucial to our survival even today

These circuits are at play when lovers meet eyes and kiss for the first time or when tears held back are sensed nonetheless; they give a lawyer the certainty that he wants that person on a jury, a negotiator the gut sense that this is the other party's final offer, and a patient the feeling she can trust her physician

In 1920, just after the first burst of enthusiasm about the then-new IQ tests, psychologist Edward Thorndike created the original formulation of 'social intelligence,' defining it in one way as 'the ability to understand and manage men and women'

Thorndike's definition by itself also allows pure manipulation to be considered a mark of interpersonal talent, and some descriptions of social intelligence make no distinction between the callow aptitudes of a con man and the genuinely caring acts that enrich healthy relationships
Being manipulative - valuing only what works for one person at the expense of the other - should not be seen as socially intelligent
Goleman considers a second, wider principle Thorndike proposed for our social aptitude: 'acting wisely in human relationships'

'Social intelligence' can be a shorthand term for being intelligent not just about our relationships but in them, broadening the focus to a two-person perspective - what emerges as a person engages in a relationship

We can take the measure of a relationship in terms of a person's impact on us, and ours on them, suggesting a new dimension of a life well lived: conducting ourselves in ways that are beneficial even at this subtle level for those with whom we connect

The social responsiveness of the brain demands that we be wise - that we realize how not just our own moods but our very biology is being driven and molded by the other people in our lives, and in turn take stock of how we affect other people's emotions and biology

assets.visual_frame_description: A municipal ledger titled Social Capital with columns for Clubs, Streets, Homes and Screens; vignettes of tantrums, ignored motorcyclists and iPod-dazed commuters fly in to be filed while a counter tallies club memberships fallen from two-thirds to one-third.
assets.player_mission: File each scene of creeping disconnection under the correct corrosion account: the Fort Worth kindergarten tantrum, the German street where nobody helps, the single-person households of 2003, Putnam's declining social capital, Rosie Garcia's headphone-stuffed customers, the vacationers who answer e-mail. For every entry record the exact statistic - the 40 percent of two-year-olds, the 24 lost minutes per Internet hour - and note the moment technology replaced the human.
key_concepts: A kindergarten teacher in Texas asked a six-year-old girl to put her toys away and she launched into a full tantrum, screaming, knocking over her chair, crawling under the teacher's desk and kicking so hard the drawers spilled out - an outburst marking an epidemic of such wildness among kindergartners documented in a single school district in Fort Worth, Texas, among poorer and better-off students alike

Even as toddlers, 40 percent of American two-year-olds watch TV for at least three hours a day - hours they are not interacting with people who can help them learn to get along better, and the more TV they watch, the more unruly they are by school age

In a German city a motorcyclist lay unmoving on the pavement after a collision for fifteen long minutes while pedestrians walked by and drivers gazed at him, until a passenger in a stopped car finally offered to call for help; a German emergency room physician commented, 'People just walk away when they see others in danger. They don't seem to care.'
In 2003 single-person households became the most common living arrangement in the United States

Robert Putnam's Bowling Alone pointed to a two-decade decline in 'social capital': while in the 1970s two-thirds of Americans belonged to organizations with regular meetings that they attended, that number had dropped to around one-third by the 1990s

A new kind of organization mushroomed from just 8,000 in the 1950s to more than 20,000 by the end of the 1990s, but membership comes via e-mail or mass mailings and the main activity boils down to sending money, not getting together

Rosie Garcia, manager of the Hot & Crusty bakery in New York's Grand Central Station, finds more and more customers utterly distracted and staring vacantly into space - she says 'Can I help you?' and they notice nothing, because their ears are stuffed with two little headphones from an iPod

Even when the headphone wearer has a one-on-one, face-to-face encounter, the sealed ears offer a ready excuse to treat the other person as an object, something to navigate around rather than someone to acknowledge - the resulting 'social autism' is an unintended human consequence of technology's invasion of daily life

A survey of American workers found that during their vacation time 34 percent checked in with their office so much that they came back as stressed - or more so - than when they left, and the cell phone can ring on a picnic with the kids

A French report of a worldwide survey of 2.5 billion viewers in seventy-two countries revealed that in 2004 people spent an average of 3 hours and 39 minutes each day watching television - Japan was highest with 4 hours and 25 minutes, and the United States came in a close second
Television, as the poet T. S. Eliot warned in 1963, 'permits millions of people to listen to the same joke at the same time, and yet remain lonesome'

A survey of 4,830 people in the United States found that for every hour people spent using the Internet, their face-to-face contact with friends, coworkers, and family fell by 24 minutes; as survey leader Norman Nie, director of the Stanford Institute for the Quantitative Study of Society, put it, 'You can't get a hug or a kiss over the Internet.'

assets.visual_frame_description: Twin scales in a dim laboratory, one heaped with warm scenes of lovers, friends and schoolrooms, the other with headphones, televisions and empty single apartments; above them a banner reads 'We are wired to connect.'
assets.player_mission: Sort each phenomenon onto the correct scale - the nourishing brain-to-brain linkup or the corrosion that deadens it: the emotional tango with the people we love most, the T-cells reshaped by chronic conflict, the iPod wearer indifferent to the stranger a foot away, the automobile's wraparound glass. key_concepts: The more strongly connected we are with someone emotionally, the greater the mutual force of priming our emotions, and our most potent exchanges occur with the people with whom we spend the greatest amount of time day in and day out, year after year - particularly those we care about the most
During these neural linkups our brains engage in an emotional tango, a dance of feelings, and relationships mold not just our experience but our biology to a surprising extent
John Cacioppo's initial research uncovered links between involvement in a distressing relationship and hikes in stress hormones to levels that damage certain genes that control virus-fighting cells

By repeatedly driving our brain into a given register, our key relationships can gradually mold certain neural circuitry - but the same finding points to reparative possibilities from our personal connections at any point in life

From the iPod wearer's perspective he is relating to someone - the singer, the band, or the orchestra plugged into his ears, his heart beating as one with theirs - but these virtual others have nothing whatever to do with the people who are just a foot or two away, to whose existence the rapt listener has become largely indifferent

'To the extent that technology absorbs people in a virtual reality, it deadens them to those who are actually nearby' - the resulting social autism adds to the list of unintended human consequences of technology
Constant digital connectivity means that even when we are on vacation, work stalks us: e-mail and cell phones penetrate essential barriers around private time and family life

The auto - a mode of passing through public space utterly insulated by wraparound glass, a half-ton or more of steel, and the lulling sound of a radio - started the process of insulation; before the auto, typical modes of travel from walking to riding a bullock cart kept travelers in easy proximity to the human world around them
Even when the one-person shell created by headphones allows a face-to-face encounter, the wearer can readily ignore anyone, looking right through them in a universal snub
The Internet has replaced television as the way free time gets used for many Americans, and we stay in touch at arm's length rather than face to face

Whenever we connect face to face (or voice to voice, or skin to skin) with someone else, our social brains interlock - the pathways of the social brain are unique in their sensitivity to the world at large

These new discoveries reveal that our relationships have subtle, yet powerful, lifelong impacts on us - that news may be unwelcome for someone whose relationships tend toward the negative, but it also points to reparative possibilities from our personal connections

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Knee, the Ground, the Smile
assets.visual_frame_description: The mosque road at dusk: kneeling soldiers, lowered rifles and a thousand faces in the balance; overhead a neural circuit glows - spindle cells, mirror neurons, a gaze releasing dopamine - as a single question hangs in the air: act wisely.
assets.player_mission: Face the final test of what it means to be intelligent about the social world: stand before the mob at the mosque and keep the whole chain of split-second social calculations from collapsing, then take Thorndike's wider principle and rule on each act you witness - callow manipulation or wisdom in a relationship. Bring the prologue to a verdict on what we create one another through before the loudspeaker dies.
key_concepts: The spotlight shifts to those ephemeral moments that emerge as we interact, and they take on deep consequence as we realize how, through their sum total, we create one another

Expanding our focus beyond the individual lets us look beyond narrow self-interest to the best interests of others, too, bringing within the scope of social intelligence capacities that enrich personal relationships, like empathy and concern

The book's inquiry speaks to questions like what makes a psychopath dangerously manipulative, whether we can do a better job of helping our children grow up to be happy, and what makes a marriage a nourishing one

Goleman first chanced upon the name of the field, 'social neuroscience,' when reading about a scientific conference on the topic held in Sweden in 2003, after years of tracking isolated findings that pointed to the neural dynamics of human relationships

Searching for the origins of the term, the earliest use Goleman found was in the early 1990s, by psychologists John Cacioppo and Gary Berntson, who back then were lone prophets of this brave new science

Cacioppo recalled, 'There was a lot of skepticism among neuroscientists about studying anything outside the cranium. Twentieth-century neuroscience thought social behavior was just too complex to study.'

Cacioppo, now director of the Center for Cognitive and Social Neuroscience at the University of Chicago, says today we can start to make sense of how the brain drives social behavior and in turn how our social world influences our brain and biology - the field has become a hot scientific topic for the twenty-first century

The emblematic research partnership in this new field is between psychologists and neuroscientists jointly using the functional MRI, or fMRI - insiders actually call MRIs 'magnets' - which adds massive computing power to yield the equivalent of a video showing what parts of the brain light up during a human moment like hearing the voice of an old friend
The social brain is the sum of the neural mechanisms that orchestrate our interactions as well as our thoughts and feelings about people and our relationships
The implications of these findings compel us to reevaluate how we live our lives, because relationships themselves take on new meaning
Before exploring the grand implications, Goleman begins with the surprising ease with which our brains interlock, spreading our emotions like a virus

Each of the isolated findings - spindle cells, mirror neurons, the dopamine gaze - offered a snapshot of the social brain, and as they accumulated the outlines of a major new discipline became visible

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Contagion Vector Scan
assets.visual_frame_description: A scanning chamber where each scene is ringed in red at the instant feeling passes from one person to another; a rhinovirus-shaped gauge labeled Contagion reads the dose, while two tracks light up beneath the scene - one wet and instant, one dry and deliberate.
assets.player_mission: Scan twelve interaction freeze-frames and detect the emotional contagion in each: the guard's fury in the lobby, the cashier's upbeat patter, the Würzburg tape's hidden mood, the audience misting at the tragic movie scene. Name the vector - the gaze, the tone, the mirroring muscle - and stamp low road or high road before the scene seals itself.
key_concepts: When someone dumps their toxic feelings on us - explodes in anger or threats, shows disgust or contempt - they activate in us circuitry for those very same distressing emotions; their act has potent neurological consequences: emotions are contagious
We 'catch' strong emotions much as we do a rhinovirus - and so can come down with the emotional equivalent of a cold

Every interaction has an emotional subtext: along with whatever else we are doing, we can make each other feel a little better, or even a lot better, or a little worse - or a lot worse, as happened to me

These tacit transactions drive what amounts to an emotional economy, the net inner gains and losses we experience with a given person, or in a given conversation, or on any given day - and by evening the net balance of feelings we have exchanged largely determines what kind of day, 'good' or 'bad,' we feel we've had
Beyond what transpires in the moment, we can retain a mood that stays with us long after the direct encounter ends - an emotional afterglow (or afterglower, in my case)

Emotional contagion is the central transaction in the emotional economy, the give-and-take of feeling that accompanies every human encounter we have, no matter what the ostensible business at hand may be

A supermarket cashier whose upbeat patter infects each of his customers in turn acts as the emotional equivalent of zeitgebers, those forces in nature that entrain our biological rhythms to their own pace
Contagion can occur with many people at one time, as visibly as when an audience mists up at a tragic movie scene, or as subtly as the tone of a meeting turning a bit testy
The amygdala, an almond-shaped area in the midbrain, triggers the fight, flight, or freeze response to danger - and of the entire range of feeling, fear most powerfully arouses the amygdala

The amygdala acts as a radar for the brain, operating the brain's early warning system, scanning everything that happens, ever vigilant for emotionally salient events - especially for potential threats
The amygdala's role as a sentinel and trigger for distress is old news to neuroscience, but its social role, as part of the brain's system for emotional contagion, has been revealed only recently
Like secondhand smoke, the leakage of emotions can make a bystander an innocent casualty of someone else's toxic state - I was an unwitting victim of that security guard's fury

assets.visual_frame_description: A skyscraper atrium with banks of elevators where a furious guard stands between you and the exit door; a taped voice reads philosophy in the corner while a mood gauge creeps upward unseen and a student's fingers push metal pins into holes in a wooden board.
assets.player_mission: Play Daniel Goleman late for a meeting, cut through the midtown Manhattan atrium, and face the uniformed guard who screams 'You can't walk through here!' and 'Private property!' - then switch seats and play the guard as your anger echoes through your own gut for blocks. End the round as the Würzburg student who must explain why her mood lifted during a taped reading of David Hume without ever knowing why.
key_concepts: As soon as Goleman reached the building's lobby with its banks of elevators, a uniformed guard stormed over, waving his arms and yelling, 'You can't walk through here!' and 'Private property! It's private property!'
Goleman's shaky attempt to reason - 'It would help if there were a sign on the door saying Do Not Enter' - made the guard even angrier: 'Get out! Get out!' he screamed
'Unsettled, I hastily beat my retreat, his anger reverberating in my own gut for the next several blocks'
Such interpersonal judo has countless variations, but they all come down to our ability to change another person's mood, and they ours
When I make you frown, I evoke in you a touch of worry; when you make me smile, I feel happy - in this clandestine exchange, emotions pass from person to person, from outside to inside

In moments of confronting someone's anger, our brain automatically scans to see if it signals some further danger, and the resulting hypervigilance is driven largely by the amygdala, whose extensive circuitry commandeers key points throughout the brain when driven by alarm

This increased amygdala-driven vigilance heightens our alertness to emotional cues in other people, and that intensified focus more powerfully evokes their feelings in us, lubricating contagion - our moments of apprehension increase our susceptibility to another person's emotions

In the experiment at the University of Würzburg in Germany, students listened to a taped voice reading a German translation of David Hume's Philosophical Essay Concerning Human Understanding in two versions, happy or sad, so subtly inflected that people were unaware of the difference unless they explicitly listened for it

Students came away from the tape either slightly happier or slightly more somber than before, with no idea their mood had shifted, let alone why - and the mood shift occurred even when they performed a distracting task, putting metal pins into holes in a wooden board, as they listened

The distraction created static for the high road, hampering intellectual understanding of the philosophical passage, but it did not lessen a whit how contagious the moods were - the low road stayed wide open

One way moods differ from the grosser feeling of emotions has to do with the ineffability of their causes: while we typically know what has triggered an outright emotion, we often find ourselves in a mood without knowing its source

As Swedish researchers found, merely seeing a picture of a happy face elicits fleeting activity in the muscles that pull the mouth into a smile - whenever we gaze at a photograph of a face displaying a strong emotion, our facial muscles automatically start to mirror it

assets.visual_frame_description: A double-entry ledger with columns for Feelings Given and Feelings Caught; each interaction arrives as a receipt - the guard's anger, the cashier's warmth, the meeting's testy tone - and at day's end the net balance glows 'good' or 'bad' in gold.
assets.player_mission: Audit a day's emotional transactions and balance the ledger of net inner gains and losses, filing each entry under contagion, afterglow, or the amygdala's hypervigilance. For every encounter record what passed between you - the worry you caught, the smile you gave - and close the books at evening with the verdict that decides whether the day was good or bad.
key_concepts: The low road is circuitry that operates beneath our awareness, automatically and effortlessly, with immense speed - most of what we do seems to be piloted by massive neural networks operating via the low road, particularly in our emotional life

The low road uses neural circuitry that runs through the amygdala and similar automatic nodes, while the high road sends inputs to the prefrontal cortex, the brain's executive center, which contains our capacity for intentionality - we can think about what's happening to us
The low road is faster than it is accurate; the high road, while slower, can help us arrive at a more accurate view of what's going on - the low road is quick and dirty, the high slow but mindful
In the words of the philosopher John Dewey, one system operates 'slam-bang, act-first and think-afterwards,' while the other is more 'wary and observant'

The speed differential between the two systems - the instant emotional one is several times faster in brain time than the more rational one - allows snap decisions we might later regret or need to justify; as Robert Heinlein wryly noted, 'Man is not a rational animal, but a rationalizing one'

The low road can be seen as 'wet,' dripping with emotion, and the high road as relatively 'dry,' coolly rational - the low road traffics in raw feelings, the high in a considered understanding of what's going on

The scene was Paris, 1895: the Lumiere brothers presented the first 'moving picture' in history, a short film of a train chugging into a station, and the utterly naive audience screamed in terror and ducked under their seats, because their brain's perceptual system registered the images as reality

In what may be the only article in the annals of neuroscience to acknowledge the help of Clint Eastwood, an Israeli research team showed clips from the 1970s spaghetti western The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly to volunteers in an fMRI and concluded the movie played the viewers' brains like a neural puppeteer

When the camera swooped in for a close-up of a face, face-recognition areas lit up; a building or vista activated the visual area that takes in physical surroundings; delicate hand movements engaged the region governing touch and movement; and scenes of gunshots, explosions and surprising plot twists roared the emotional centers into action

Whatever happened in one viewer's brain occurred in lockstep in the others, moment by moment throughout the film - the action onscreen choreographed the identical inner dance in everyone watching, for as a maxim in social science holds, 'A thing is real if it is real in its consequences'

The one major exception to this puppetry was the high-road prefrontal areas, which house the brain's executive centers and facilitate critical thinking, including the thought 'This is just a movie' - and so today we do not run in panic as an onscreen train roars toward us, despite the fear welling up inside

In the Stanford experiment on emotional suppression, the woman who suppressed her feelings after the harrowing Hiroshima-Nagasaki documentary felt tense and ill at ease and her blood pressure rose steadily - but the woman who was open and honest exhibited the same steady rise, because the tension was not just palpable but contagious

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: The Low and High Roads
assets.visual_frame_description: A two-lane freeway of the mind: a wet, fast lane thundering with screams, smiles and the train of 1895 Paris; a dry, slow lane where a man studies a face and decides; over both, a movie screen plays The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly and the viewers' brains light up in lockstep.
assets.player_mission: Sort each mechanism onto its road: the amygdala's lightning read of a scowl, the mirroring smile, the subliminal Hume tape and the truth that leaks through the face onto the low road; deliberate trust judgments, the composition of a lie and the thought 'this is just a movie' onto the high. Justify every placement with its speed and accuracy before the puppeteer's credits roll.
key_concepts: Forthrightness is the brain's default response: our neural wiring transmits our every minor mood onto the muscles of our face, making our feelings instantly visible - the display of emotion is automatic and unconscious, and so its suppression demands conscious effort
The facial muscles are controlled by the low road, the choice to lie by the high road; in an emotional lie, the face belies what's said - the high road conceals, the low road reveals

Our warning system for whether we can trust someone has two branches, high and low: the high road operates when we intentionally make a judgment of whether someone might be trustworthy, while a continual amygdala-driven appraisal goes on outside our awareness, regardless of whether we consciously think about the issue

Neurological patients with extensive amygdala damage are unable to make judgments of how trustworthy someone might be - shown a photo of a man ordinary people find highly suspicious, they rate him on a par with the man others rated most deserving of their trust

In the tragic-story study, if the actor's face showed an appropriate sadness the listener's amygdala and related circuits for sadness activated, but if the actor's face was smiling during the sad tale - an emotional mismatch - the listener's brain activated a site specializing in vigilance for social threats or conflicting information, and the listeners actively disliked the person telling the story

This circuitry specialized for suspicion differs from that for empathy and rapport, and evolutionary theory holds that our ability to sense when we should be suspicious has been every bit as essential for human survival as our capacity for trust and cooperation

Lying demands conscious, intentional activity in the high road, which handles the executive control systems that keep our words and deeds smoothly on track - liars pay most attention to their choice of words, censoring what they say, and less to their choice of facial expression

Attention is a limited capacity, and telling a lie demands an extra dose - this extra allocation of neural resources leaves the prefrontal area less wherewithal to perform another task: inhibiting involuntary displays of emotion that might betray that lie

Paul Ekman, a world-class expert on detecting lies from a person's demeanor, told Goleman, 'There is no surefire lie detector... But you can detect hot spots' - points where a person's emotions don't fit the words, signs of extra mental effort whose reasons can range from simple nervousness to bald-faced lying

When a person tells a lie in answering a question, he begins his response about two-tenths of a second later than does a person telling the truth - that gap signifies the effort to compose the lie well

Experts on emotion tell us we ordinarily avert our eyes downward with sadness, away with disgust, and down or away while feeling guilt or shame - but the believe-what-I'm-saying eyelock reveals little about whether someone is telling the truth; it may be more about rapport-building than lying

Giovanni Vigliotto, who may have married one hundred wealthy women over his romantic career, was undone by Patricia Gardner, who admitted that what attracted her was 'that honest trait': he looked her directly in the eyes, smiling, even as he lied through his teeth

assets.visual_frame_description: A stark Stanford conversation lab where two women talk after a harrowing film; a blood-pressure monitor climbs behind each of them, and on the far wall a suave con man holds a courtroom stare, his smile fixed as the high road composes and the low road leaks.
assets.player_mission: Sit in the Stanford suppression experiment as the woman who must hide her horror at the Hiroshima and Nagasaki documentary, and then as the woman who cannot - keep your face neutral while your blood pressure climbs and the other woman's climbs with you. Then face Giovanni Vigliotto across a courtroom and read his confident eyelock for hot spots before he adds another bride.
key_concepts: At Stanford University, two women who were complete strangers had just watched a harrowing documentary of the poignant human aftermath of the nuclear bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki - one was utterly frank about her upset, while the other, a volunteer instructed to hide her true feelings, suppressed her emotions and feigned indifference

The emotionally open woman felt 'off' with her partner as they talked, sensing this was someone she would not want as a friend; the one who suppressed her true feelings felt tense and ill at ease, distracted and preoccupied

Suppressing disturbing feelings takes a physiological toll: the suppressor's blood pressure rose steadily as the conversation went on, reflecting the emotional effort - but the woman who was open and honest exhibited the same steady rise, because the tension was contagious

The act of lying demands conscious, intentional activity in the high road, which handles the executive control systems that manage the emotional and physical channels through which truth might inadvertently leak - successful lying takes concentration
In the interpersonal flow of emotion, power matters: in a romantic couple, one partner will make a larger emotional shift to converge with the other - the partner who has less power

Couples tacitly negotiate which partner will have more power in what domain - one may be dominant in finances, and the other in social scheduling - but in the realm of emotions the less powerful partner all in all makes the greater internal adjustments in their emotional convergence

Since Freud's time psychotherapists have noticed that their own body mirrors emotions their clients are feeling - if a client cries over a painful recollection, the therapist will feel tears well up; if she is terrified by a traumatic memory, feelings of fear will stir in the pit of the therapist's stomach

Freud pointed out that attuning themselves to their own body gives psychoanalysts a window into their clients' emotional world, and great psychotherapists go a step further, picking up emotional undertones from patients who have not even allowed these feelings into their own consciousness

New statistical methods and computing power allowed scientists to analyze an immense number of data points, from heart rate and the like, during a live interaction - revealing that when a married couple argues, each partner's body tends to mimic the disturbances in the other, driving each other into escalating states of anger, hurt, and sadness

Marital researchers videotaped couples arguing, then invited total strangers to watch the tapes and guess which emotions one partner was feeling - as the volunteers guessed, their own physiology tracked those they were watching, and the more strongly a stranger's body mimicked the person she watched, the more accurate was her sense of what that person felt

The mimicry effect was most marked for negative emotions like anger, and people whose own faces showed the strongest expressions were the most accurate at judging the feelings of others - empathy seems to be as physiological as it is mental, built on sharing the inner state of the other person

The general principle: the more similar the physiological state of two people at a given moment, the more easily they can sense each other's feelings - and since the emotions we catch have consequences, we have good reason to understand how to shift them for the better

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Rapport Triad Detector
assets.visual_frame_description: A dark playback room where two wiggling lines - blue for patient, green for therapist - undulate beneath each video frame; a triad gauge lights Mutual Attention, Good Feeling, Coordination as the lines mesh into a graceful ballet.
assets.player_mission: Scan pairs of scenes from Carl Marci's videotaped therapy sessions and detect the three ingredients of rapport - mutual attention, shared positive feeling, coordinated duet - in each. Ring the instant the blue and green sweat-response lines stop flying like jittery birds and start flying like birds in formation, and stamp each moment rapport or discord.
key_concepts: In the first psychotherapy session, the psychiatrist sat stiffly formal in a wooden armchair while his patient slumped on a leather couch, her very air one of defeat; he made a therapeutic gaffe, cut the patient off, talked over her, and the session wobbled on, off-key and out of synch

In the second session, Patient Number Two had proposed to his longtime girlfriend - now fiancée - the day before, and therapist and patient quietly exulted together, their mood upbeat and their rapport so thick that their posture and movements mirrored each other as though intentionally choreographed
When the therapist shifted one foot and then the other in the rapport session, the patient immediately did the same

Both therapy sessions were captured on videotape with two rectangular metal boxes stacked like stereo components between therapist and client, extruding wires to a metal clip each person wore on a fingertip that streamed readings of subtle shifts in their sweat response as they spoke
The videos depict the continuous readings as a wiggling line floating under each person, blue for the patient, green for the therapist, undulating with rising and falling emotions
During the anxious, jarring exchanges of the first session, the two lines moved like jittery birds, their ups and downs on private trajectories - they etched a portrait of disconnection

But during the rapport of the second session, the lines flew like birds in formation, a graceful ballet of coordinated movement - when two people feel rapport, the gliding lines reveal, their very physiology attunes

Carl Marci, a psychiatrist at Harvard Medical School, conducted the study, lugging a suitcase filled with monitoring gear to the offices of willing therapists all over the Boston area, joining an elect group of pioneers crossing the once-impregnable barrier of the skull

Marci has extracted from his data what he calls a 'logarithm for empathy' - a mathematical equation that reduces to precise numbers the pattern of two people's physiology at that peak of rapport when one feels understood by the other

Robert Rosenthal, Goleman's statistical methods professor at Harvard and by reputation just about the most likable professor in the entire department, had a gift for emotional uplift - people came out of his office feeling heard, understood, and almost magically better
Rapport, Rosenthal has found, always entails three elements: mutual attention, shared positive feeling, and a well-coordinated nonverbal duet - as these three arise in tandem, we catalyze rapport

Shared attention is the first essential ingredient: as two people attend to what the other says and does, they generate a sense of mutual interest, a joint focus that amounts to perceptual glue, and one indicator of rapport is mutual empathy - both partners experience being experienced

assets.visual_frame_description: A bustling restaurant at noon where every table sets its own tempo; the waitress moves from the dark corner of a nursing drink to the hilarity of a booth, her posture, pace and voice gliding into each patron's wavelength.
assets.player_mission: Play the waitress every restaurant loves: match the morose man's quiet in the dark corner, the coworkers' laughter at the lunch-hour booth, the young mom's frenzy with two hyperactive toddlers, and glide into each customer's rhythm to earn the biggest tips in the place. Then play the NYU confederate and feel the difference between mimicry that is spontaneous and mimicry that is mechanical - find out which one gets you liked.
key_concepts: At a local restaurant there's a waitress everyone loves to have serve them - she has an uncanny knack for matching the mood and pace of her customers: quiet and discreet with the morose man nursing a drink in the dark corner, sociable and outgoing with a noisy batch of coworkers, wading into the frenzy of a young mom with two hyperactive toddlers - and she gets by far the biggest tips of any
The more two people unconsciously synchronize their movements and mannerisms during their interaction, the more positively they will feel about their encounter - and about each other

In the experiments at New York University, volunteers judging a series of photos sat with another student who was actually a confederate of the researchers, instructed to either smile or not, to shake his foot or rub his face - and whatever the confederate did, the volunteers tended to mimic: face-rubbing elicited face-rubbing, a smile primed a smile in return
Careful questioning revealed that the volunteers had no idea they had been smiling or shaking their foot in imitation, nor had they noticed the choreographed mannerisms

When the confederate intentionally mimicked the motions and gestures of the person he was talking with, he was not particularly liked - but when the confederate was spontaneous in his mimicry, he was found more appealing

Contrary to the advice of popular books on the matter, intentionally matching someone - imitating the position of their arms, say, or taking on their posture - does not in itself heighten rapport; such mechanical, faked synchrony feels off

In building a sense of positivity, the nonverbal messages we send can matter more than what we are saying: in an experiment where managers gave people unflattering feedback while still exhibiting warm feelings toward them through their voice and expression, those receiving the critiques nevertheless felt positively about the overall interaction

People in rapport are animated, freely expressing their emotions - their spontaneous, immediate responsiveness has the look of a closely choreographed dance, their eyes meet, their bodies get close, chairs get pulled near, even their noses get closer than is typical during conversation, and they are comfortable with silences
Lacking coordination, a conversation will feel uncomfortable, with mistimed responses or awkward pauses - people fidget or freeze, and such mismatches torpedo rapport

One acting coach assigns his students to watch entire movies with the sound off, to study the silent dance - the elegant orchestration of movements, smooth turn-taking, even coordination of gazes that the naked eye can otherwise miss

Studies where friends in conversation wore sensors that monitored breathing patterns found the listener's breathing roughly mirroring that of the speaker - inhaling as the partner exhaled, or matching by breathing together - and this respiratory synchrony heightens as the moment to switch speakers approaches
During those frequent moments of levity when close friends talk, both begin laughing at virtually the same moment, and during the laughter the rhythm of their breathing aligns remarkably

assets.visual_frame_description: A clockwork laboratory where pendulums swing into synch; two cellists' brains glow in synchrony across hemispheres, breathing waveforms align above a conversation, and a chorus of metronomes ticks the invisible dance into being.
assets.player_mission: Audit the inner timekeepers: file every timing mechanism under the oscillators that reset to the periodicity of an incoming signal - the cellists' right hemispheres, the breathing that mirrors the speaker, the body movements that punctuate speech within a fraction of a second. For each entry, log the beat: the ninety-five-mile-per-hour pitch, the stadium wave, the pas de deux.
key_concepts: Whenever we find ourselves in harmony with someone else, we can thank what neuroscientists call 'oscillators' - neural systems that act like clocks, resetting over and over their rate of firing to coordinate with the periodicity of an incoming signal
That signal may be as simple as the rate at which a friend hands you the dishes she's washed so you can dry them, or as complex as the movements in a well-choreographed pas de deux

Nature loves good timing: when waves are out of synch, they cancel each other; when they synchronize, they amplify - and in the interpersonal realm, our emotional rhythms entrain, so when a human zeitgeber draws us into an upbeat range, they do us a favor

If two cellists had their neural activity measured during their rapture playing the same bit of music, the rhythms of neuronal firing in their right hemispheres would be extraordinarily close - the synchrony of these zones for musical abilities is far greater across the two brains than between the left and right hemispheres within each brain

The best comedians display an effortless sense of rhythm - as the joke runs, 'Ask me why I can't tell a good joke... Poor timing' - and like concert musicians examining a musical score, they can analyze precisely how many beats to pause before delivering a punch line

Frame-by-frame analyses of pairs talking reveal how each person's movements punctuate their conversation's rhythm, with head and hand actions coinciding with stress points and hesitations in speech - and such body-to-speech synchronies occur within a fraction of a second

The body is like the brain's puppet: the brain's clock ticks in milliseconds, or even tinier microseconds, while our conscious information processing and our thoughts about it lope along seconds at a time

Even a bit of peripheral vision offers enough information about a body-to-body linkage to set up a coupled oscillation - walk with someone and within minutes both of you will be moving your hands and legs in perfect harmony, just as two pendulums swinging freely come into synch

The neural math of entrainment applies whenever we time our movements to the outer world - not just with other people but when intercepting a soccer ball at top speed, or hitting a ninety-five-mile-per-hour pitch
The rhythmic undertones and fluid synchrony of even the barest interactions can be as remarkably complex as the improvised coordination of jazz - the entrainment goes far beyond nodding

Even in the womb, infants synchronize their movements to the rhythms of human speech, though not to other sounds, and one-year-olds match the timing and duration of their baby talk to the beat of their mother's speaking

Oscillators echo the neural equivalent of the ditty from Alice's Adventures in Wonderland - 'Will you, won't you, will you, won't you, will you join the dance?' - putting us in synch unconsciously, like the flowing ease with which lovers approach for an embrace or take each other's hands at just the right instant as they walk down the street

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: In Synch or Out
assets.visual_frame_description: A sorting gallery where pairs of figures step onto a dance floor that glows green when their movements mesh and red when they jitter apart; a banner reads 'Mismatches torpedo rapport.'
assets.player_mission: Sort each moment into In Synch or Out: the knee-shifting therapist and patient, the jittery birds of the failed session, the phone call with its studied turn-taking, the long pause that stays smooth because the bodies still mesh. Then rule on the deepest case - which synchronies are spontaneous, and which mechanical fakes feel off?
key_concepts: Any conversation operates on two levels, high road and low: the high road traffics in rationality, words, and meanings, while the low expresses a free-form vitality that runs beneath the words, holding the interaction together through an immediately felt connection

The sense of connection hinges less on what's said than on the more direct and intimate, unspoken emotional link - a constant silent chatter that offers a between-the-lines narrative, letting the other person know how we feel from moment to moment and adjust accordingly

Whenever two people converse, we can see the emotional minuet played out in the dance of flashing eyebrows, rapid hand gestures, fleeting facial expressions, swiftly adjusted word pacing, and shifts of gaze

Synchrony telegraphs a tacit understanding or agreement between the speaker and listener, and the reassuring harmonization tends to continue during rough patches like long pauses, interruptions, and simultaneous speaking - even when a conversation frays or lapses into silence, physical synchrony maintains the sense that the interaction persists nonetheless

A conversation that lacks reassuring physical synchrony has to be even smoother in its verbal coordination to feel harmonious - when people cannot see each other, as in a phone call or over an intercom, their pattern of speaking and taking turns tends to become more studiedly coordinated

One study tracked postural shifts among students in a classroom: the more similar their postures were to their teacher's, the more strongly they felt rapport and the greater their overall level of involvement - posture matching may offer a quick reading of classroom atmosphere

Getting in synch can be a visceral pleasure, and the larger the group, the better - the aesthetic expression of group synch appears in the universal enjoyment of dancing or moving together to a beat, and in arms that swing as one in a 'wave' sweeping through a stadium

The wiring for such resonance seems built into the human nervous system - the very ability to resonate, even in babies, points to an underlying wiring in the brain that makes all this synchrony so natural
When our attention is split, we tune out a bit, missing crucial details - especially emotional ones; seeing eye to eye opens a pathway for empathy

Social psychologists have found again and again that the more two people naturally make coupled moves - simultaneous, at a similar tempo, or otherwise coordinated - the greater their positive feelings

The more synchrony occurs, the more alike the emotions both partners will feel; getting in synch creates an emotional match, as when a baby and mother move in tandem from a low level of energy and alertness to a higher one and their shared pleasure steadily heightens

In Rosenthal's study, one of each pair of people, secretly working with the researchers, showed the difference between mere social ease and full rapport: in social ease we feel comfortable, but we do not have the sense of the other person tuning in to our feelings - Bob was fully present to us, paying utter attention

assets.visual_frame_description: A warm kitchen where a mother's face widens into a smile and her baby's lips relax toward a grin; a metronome pulses at adagio while sound-wave contours of Motherese undulate between them like a melody being composed in real time.
assets.player_mission: Take the mother's side of the protoconversation: hold your baby's gaze, time your Motherese to its 300-hertz contours, and keep the duet's adagio pulse at about 90 beats per minute as your baby's smile builds across three seconds. Fail the timing and watch the baby withdraw, look puzzled, then distress - hold the rhythm and end matched, typically happy, in an 'immediate, unverbalized, conceptless, rapport.'
key_concepts: Picture a mother holding her baby: the mother makes an affectionate 'kissy-face,' pursing her lips, and the baby draws his lips inward in a somewhat sober expression; the mother widens her mouth into a slight smile, the baby relaxes his lips, and both join in a slight smile before the baby breaks into a full-blown beam - the entire interaction takes less than three seconds
Such rudimentary engagements are called 'protoconversation' - the prototype of all human interaction, communication at its most basic

Microanalysis reveals that babies and mothers precisely time the start, end, and pauses in their baby talk, creating a coupling of rhythm - each captures and coordinates what they do with the timing of the other

These 'conversations' are nonverbal, resorting to words only as sound effects - we engage through our gaze, touch, and tone of voice, with messages going via smiles and coos and most especially 'Motherese,' the adult complement to baby talk
More like a song than a sentence, Motherese deploys prosody, melodic overtones of speech that transcend culture and are much the same whether the mother speaks Mandarin Chinese, Urdu, or English

Motherese always sounds friendly and playful, with a high pitch - around 300 hertz, to be technical - and short, spiked, undulating or gliding pitch contours, and often a mother will synchronize Motherese with patting or stroking her baby in a repeated, periodic rhythm

The mother-infant pirouettes are short, a matter of just seconds or even milliseconds - paced by a steady adagio pulse at about 90 beats per minute - and they end when both partners match states, typically happy ones

Colwyn Trevarthen of the University of Edinburgh, made the world expert on protoconversation by painstaking examination of endless hours of videotaped mother-infant interactions, describes the duet as one where both performers 'seek harmony and counterpoint on one beat to create a melody'

The frequency of the mother's touch and the sound of her voice give the baby the reassuring message of her love - resulting, as Trevarthen puts it, in an 'immediate, unverbalized, conceptless, rapport'

If the mother pays too little attention or responds without enthusiasm, the baby reacts by withdrawing; if the mother's responses are poorly timed, the baby will look puzzled, then distressed; and if it's the baby who fails to respond, the mother in turn will get upset

The protoconversation marks a baby's first lesson in how to interact - we learn how to synchronize emotionally long before we have words for those feelings, and the ability to get into synch as we did when we were babies serves us through life, guiding every social interaction

Just as feelings were the main topic of protoconversation for us as infants, they remain the bedrock of communication in adulthood - this silent dialogue on feelings is the substrate on which all other encounters build and the hidden agenda in every interaction

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Mirror Neuron Sweep
assets.visual_frame_description: A neuro-imaging bay where a single laser-thin electrode trace flickers across each frame; a monkey watches an assistant lift a cone to his lips, and a red spike marks the exact cell that lights in his sensorimotor cortex.
assets.player_mission: Scan a grid of moments and detect the mirror neurons at work in each: the monkey watching the ice-cream cone, the awake patient's single neuron firing at another's pinprick, the toddler's unbidden smile, the locked rhythms of two cellists. Name the mirror signature - anticipation, intention, emotion - and ring it before the feed cuts.
key_concepts: Neuroscientists stumbled on mirror neurons by accident in 1992 while mapping the sensorimotor area of monkeys' brains with electrodes so laser-thin they could be implanted in single brain cells - some neurons lit up only when the monkey was grasping something, others only when it was tearing it apart

The unexpected discovery came one hot afternoon when a research assistant came back from a break eating an ice-cream cone: the scientists were astonished to see a sensorimotor cell activate as one monkey watched the assistant lift the cone to his lips

In a remarkable study where a laser-thin electrode monitored a single neuron in an awake person, the neuron fired both when the person performed an action and when merely watching someone else do it - and it fired both when the person anticipated a pinprick and when merely seeing someone else receive a pinprick, a neural snapshot of primal empathy in action

Many mirror neurons operate in the premotor cortex, which governs activities ranging from speaking and movement to simply intending to act; because they are adjacent to motor neurons, the areas of the brain that initiate a movement can readily begin to activate even as we watch someone else make that same movement
Simulating an act is, in the brain, the same as performing it, except that the actual execution is somehow blocked

The human brain harbors multiple mirror neuron systems - not just for mimicking actions but for reading intentions, for extracting the social implications from what someone does, and for reading emotions

When volunteers lay in an fMRI watching a video showing someone smile or scowl, most brain areas that activated in the observers were the same as those active in the person displaying the emotion, though not as extreme

Mirror neurons make emotions contagious, letting the feelings we witness flow through us, helping us get in synch and follow what's going on - we 'feel' the other in the broadest sense, sensing their sentiments, their movements, their sensations, their emotions as they act inside us

Mirror neurons respond to the mere hint of an intention to move, and they help us track what motivation may be in play - sensing what other people intend, and why, lets us keep a step ahead of whatever will happen next, like social chameleons

Mirror neurons appear to be essential to the way children learn: imitative learning has long been recognized as a major avenue of childhood development, and as children watch, mirror neurons etch in their own brains a repertoire for emotion, for behavior, and for how the world works

Giacomo Rizzolatti, the Italian neuroscientist who discovered mirror neurons, explains that these systems 'allow us to grasp the minds of others not through conceptual reasoning but through direct simulation; by feeling, not by thinking'

Neuroscientists call the mutually reverberating state of two linked brains 'empathic resonance' - a brain-to-brain linkage that forms a two-person circuitry via the low road, creating an immediacy, a sense of sharing the moment

assets.visual_frame_description: A bright grocery aisle where a toddler looks up at a smiling lady; behind them the figure of Daniel Stern observes a mother and infant, and a caption reads 'constructed to be captured by the nervous systems of others.'
assets.player_mission: Play two-year-old Goleman in the grocery store aisle, and then the lady whose warm smile pulls his mouth into an unbidden grin - feel the strings that work your face without your say-so. Then sit across from Daniel Stern at the University of Geneva and let him show you how your nervous system is constructed to be captured by another's, until your mind feels permeable.
key_concepts: Goleman remembers being just two or three years old, wandering down the aisle of the local grocery store at his mother's side, when a lady spotted him and gave him a warm smile - his own mouth startled him by involuntarily moving into a smile in return, his face 'puppetlike, drawn by mysterious strings' that widened the muscles around his mouth and puffed out his cheeks

That unbidden reaction signaled the activity of mirror neurons - neurons that reflect back an action we observe in someone else, making us mimic that action or have the impulse to do so, the 'do-as-she-does' neurons behind the old lyric 'When you're smiling, the whole world smiles with you'

When we mentally rehearse an action - making a dry run of a talk we have to give, or envisioning the fine points of our golf swing - the same neurons activate in the premotor cortex as if we had uttered those words or made that swing

Our mirror neurons fire as we watch someone else scratch their head or wipe away a tear, so that a portion of the pattern of neuronal firing in our brain mimics theirs, mapping the identical information onto our own motor neurons and letting us participate in the other person's actions as if we were executing them
By mimicking what another person does or feels, mirror neurons create a shared sensibility, bringing the outside inside us - to understand another, we become like the other, at least a bit
Human mirror neurons are far more flexible and diverse than those in monkeys, reflecting our sophisticated social abilities

Daniel Stern, an American psychiatrist working at the University of Geneva who has made systematic observations of mothers and infants for decades, concludes that our nervous systems 'are constructed to be captured by the nervous systems of others, so that we can experience others as if from within their skin'

We can no longer, Stern adds, 'see our minds as so independent, separate and isolated' - we must view them as 'permeable,' continually interacting as though joined by an invisible link, and at least for the moment our mental life is cocreated in an interconnected two-person matrix

Mirror neurons ensure that the moment someone sees an emotion expressed on your face, they will at once sense that same feeling within themselves - our emotions are experienced not merely by ourselves in isolation but also by those around us, both covertly and openly

Stern suggests that the neurons for mimicry are at play whenever we sense another person's state of mind and resonate with their feelings - this interbrain linkage makes bodies move in tandem, thoughts go down the same roads, and emotions run along the same lines
As mirror neurons bridge brains, they create a tacit duet that opens the way for subtle but powerful transactions
Social skill depends on mirror neurons: echoing what we observe in another person prepares us to make a speedy and fitting response

assets.visual_frame_description: A facial-muscle atlas in a mirrored room where eighteen smile templates overlay a single face; each classified smile glows green or red - evoking or cold - while a counter records that happy faces are recognized more readily and quickly than negative ones.
assets.player_mission: Audit the smile inventory: classify every smile you scan - the miserable paste, the cruel relish, the supercilious hallmark, the genuine spark - by the fifteen facial muscles that compose it, and log which ones evoke a smile in return. Then file each emotion under the happy-face advantage and note the brain's bias for positive faces.
key_concepts: When Goleman first met Paul Ekman in the 1980s, Ekman had just spent a year gazing into a mirror while learning to voluntarily control each one of the close to two hundred muscles of the face, applying a mild electrical shock to locate some hard-to-detect facial muscles
Ekman has identified eighteen kinds of smiles, all various permutations of the fifteen facial muscles involved
A miserable smile pastes over an unhappy expression, like a grin-and-bear-it comment on feeling dismal
A cruel smile shows that the person relishes being angry and mean
The supercilious smile, which was Charlie Chaplin's hallmark, draws on a muscle most people can't move deliberately - a smile that, as Ekman puts it, 'smiles at smiling'

There are also genuine smiles of spontaneous pleasure or amusement - the smiles that are most likely to evoke one in return, signaling the work of mirror neurons dedicated to detecting smiles and triggering our own
As a Tibetan saying has it, 'When you smile at life, half the smile is for your face, the other half for somebody else's.'

Smiles have an edge over all other emotional expressions: the human brain prefers happy faces, recognizing them more readily and quickly than those with negative expressions - an effect known as the 'happy face advantage'

Some neuroscientists suggest that the brain has a system for positive feelings that stays primed for activity, causing people to be in upbeat moods more often than negative and to have a more positive outlook on life - implying that Nature tends to foster positive relationships
Laughter may be the shortest distance between two brains - an unstoppable infectious spread that builds an instant social bond

Pairs of complete strangers assigned to play silly games together - one person talking through a straw while directing the other, wearing a blindfold, to toss a Nerf ball back and forth - invariably fell into guffaws at their haplessness and felt a strong, immediate sense of closeness after just a few minutes; when strangers played the same games without the blindfold and straw, they never cracked a smile

Take two teenage girls giggling together: the more giddily playful the two teen best friends become, the more synchronous, animated, and happy they feel together - they resonate, and what to a parent may seem an ungodly racket is, for the teenagers making it, one of their most bonding moments

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: The Meme Sorting Room
assets.visual_frame_description: A sorting room where ideas arrive as glowing strands modeled on genes, each seeking a mind to replicate in; cue words stack into two piles - interrupters and waiters - while a Chekhovian revolver hangs on the wall, primed.
assets.player_mission: Sort each message into the meme sorting room: rap lyrics with oscillator-riveting beats, the cue words 'rude' and 'considerate,' Chekhov's gun on the wall, the whisper that begets a whisper, the camera that jumps between two minds. For each, judge the meme's power to prime action through the low road before the priming test runs.
key_concepts: Rap lyrics, like any poem, essay, or news story, can be seen as delivery systems for 'memes' - ideas that spread from mind to mind, much as emotions do - and the notion of a meme was modeled on that of a gene, an entity that replicates itself by getting passed on from person to person

Memes with particular power, like 'democracy' or 'cleanliness,' lead us to act in a specific way - they are ideas with impact; some memes naturally oppose others, and when they do, those memes are at war, a battle of ideas
Memes seem to gather power from the low road, through their association with strong emotions - an idea matters to us to the extent that it moves us, and that is precisely what emotions do
The low-road force of rap lyrics, made all the stronger by oscillator-riveting beats, may gather special force - certainly more than they would if read on a page

In the priming experiment, one group of volunteers heard cue words referring to impoliteness, such as 'rude' and 'obnoxious,' while another heard words like 'considerate' and 'polite' - two out of three primed for rudeness butted in to interrupt, while eight of ten primed for politeness waited the full ten minutes for the conversation to end

As the Russian playwright Anton Chekhov famously put it, never put a gun on the wall in the second act of a play without using it by the end of the third - because simply thinking of an action prepares the mind to perform it, and the audience will be expecting gunshots

Priming guides us through our daily routines without mental effort, something like a mental to-do list - seeing our toothbrush on the bathroom sink in the morning cues us to automatically reach for it and start brushing

This urge to enact guides us everywhere: when someone whispers to us, we whisper back, and talk about a Grand Prix race to someone driving on a highway, and he will speed up - it's as though one brain implants similar feelings, thoughts, and impulses in the other

Such mental intimacy bespeaks an emotional closeness - the more satisfied and communicative a couple, the more accurate their mutual mindreading, and when we know someone well or experience strong rapport, conditions are near optimal for a confluence of our internal thoughts, feelings, perceptions, and memories

On a tropical island, Goleman spotted a graceful four-masted ship and snapped the first photo he'd taken in ten days; hours later, out of the blue, his wife asked, 'Did you bring the camera?' as though she had read his mind - such synchronicities stem from the verbal equivalent of emotional contagion, with trains of association primed on set tracks beyond the reach of active attention

Researchers at Berkeley recruited new roommates and tracked their emotional responses as they separately watched short films - one a hilarious Robin Williams comedy, another a tearjerker depicting a boy crying at the death of his father; on first viewing the roommates reacted as differently as any pair of random strangers, but seven months later their reactions had converged strikingly

Darryl McDaniels, the DMC in Run-DMC, complained that rap's themes of parties, guns and women had nothing to say to him from nine to bedtime, heralding reformed rappers like John Stevens (known as Legend), who holds a degree from the University of Pennsylvania, and Kanye West, son of a college professor, who observes, 'My mom's a teacher, and I'm kind of a teacher too'
