assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Crowd Contagion Ramp
assets.visual_frame_description: A European stadium terrace packed with chanting fans where flags wave in unison; a lone gang leader edges toward the rival section as a contagion line races through the crowd; beside it, a boardroom where a calm actor tips a group's mood and the bonus ledger bends with it.
assets.player_mission: Stand at the edge of the superhooligan flashpoint and manage mass contagion: hold the chants from turning to threats, read the moment the gang leader attacks a rival fan, and decide whether the crowd's mirror-neuron synchrony sweeps toward violence or toward the shared field of a great performance. Then run the Yale bonus meeting and keep a secret actor's planted mood from biasing every decision in the room.
key_concepts: They call them 'superhooligans,' the gangs of soccer fans who spark riots and mass fights at European matches - and the formula for a soccer riot is the same, no matter the country, repeated over and over since the early 1980s with tragic consequences

The formula: a small, tight-knit gang of fans arrives hours early and goes on a drinking binge; as crowds gather, the gangs get caught up in waving team flags and chanting; the superhooligans gravitate to points where their team's fans mix with those of their rivals, and the chants change to outright threats

Then comes the flashpoint, when a gang leader attacks a rival fan, triggering others to join in, and the fights spread - in a drunken belligerent mob the alcohol disinhibits neural controls over impulses, so the moment a leader models the first carnage, contagion primes the rest to follow

Elias Canetti, in his study Crowds and Power, observes that what coalesces a mass of individuals into a crowd is their domination by a 'single passion' everyone shares - a common emotion that leads to united action: collective contagion
A mood can sweep through a group with great rapidity - a remarkable display of the parallel alignment of biological subsystems that puts everyone there in physiological synchrony

The swiftness of shifts in the activity of crowds looks suspiciously like mirror neuron coordination writ large, and crowd decision-making goes on within seconds - presumably the time it takes for person-to-person transmission of mirror neuron synchrony to sweep through

Group contagion in its more sedate forms can be witnessed at any great performance, where actors or musicians create a field effect, playing the audience's emotions like instruments - plays, concerts, and movies let us enter a shared field of emotions with large numbers of strangers

Looping together in an upbeat register is, as psychologists like to say, 'inherently reinforcing' - it makes everyone feel good - and crowd contagion goes on even in the most minimal of groups: three people sitting face to face with each other in silence, where in the absence of a power hierarchy the person with the most emotionally expressive face sets the shared tone

In a now-classic study at Yale University, volunteers were put in groups to decide how much of an end-of-year bonus to give each employee, and one participant in each meeting was actually a seasoned actor whose secret assignment was to be confrontational and downbeat with some of the groups, and helpful and upbeat with the others

In whichever direction the actor's emotions went, his lead was followed - the group members showed a distinct shift in their own mood, becoming upset or feeling pleasant accordingly, but none of them seemed to know why their mood had changed; unwittingly, they had been looped into a mood shift

The feelings that pass through a group can bias how all the group members process information and hence the decisions they make - any group coming to a decision together would do well to attend not just to what's being said, but to the shared emotions in the room as well

This convergence bespeaks a subtle, inexorable magnetism - a gravitylike pull toward thinking and feeling alike about things in general among people who are in close relationships of any kind, family members, workmates, and friends

assets.visual_frame_description: A city sidewalk rendered as a diagnostic board where passersby are grey silhouettes; the man slumped in pain glows red until one figure stops, and a circle of concern spreads green across the concrete while a gauge labeled Attention swings from trance to focus.
assets.player_mission: Scan the street scenes and detect attention or its absence in each: the moaning man in the seminary doorway, the shirtless man stepped over on the subway stairs, the homeless man ignored for the petition woman. Ring the moment attention is paid - the stop, the pause, the turned head - and judge the trade-off of the urban trance before the scene resets.
key_concepts: One afternoon at the Princeton Theological Seminary, forty students waited to give a short practice sermon on which they would be rated - half assigned random biblical topics, the other half the parable of the Good Samaritan, and none knew they were taking part in an experiment on altruism

The seminarians' route passed directly by a doorway in which a man was slumped, groaning in evident pain - twenty-four of the forty students passed right by, ignoring the plaintive moans, and those who were mulling over the lessons of the Good Samaritan's tale were no more likely to stop and help than any of the others
Time mattered: among ten seminarians who thought they were late to give their sermon, only one stopped; among another ten who thought they had plenty of time, six offered help
A critical factor in altruism is simply taking the time to pay attention - our empathy is strongest to the degree we fully focus on someone and so loop emotionally

People on busy city streets worldwide are less likely to notice, greet, or offer help to someone else because of what has been called the 'urban trance' - a self-absorbed state we fall into on crowded streets to gird against stimulus overload, shutting out the compelling needs of those around us along with the distractions

A homeless person sitting dejectedly on the street of an American city asking for money may receive no attention from passersby, who a few steps away will gladly listen and respond to a well-dressed, outgoing woman asking for signatures on a political petition

One rush hour in New York City, a shabby, shirtless man lay sprawled across the stairs at the Times Square subway station, motionless, eyes closed - no one seemed to notice, and people simply stepped over his body in their rush to get home

The moment Goleman stopped to see what was wrong, other people stopped too: almost instantly a small circle of concern formed, a man went to a hot dog stand to get food, a woman scurried to get a bottle of water, another summoned a subway patrol officer who radioed for help - within minutes the man was revived, eating happily, and waiting for an ambulance
The man spoke only Spanish, had no money, and had been wandering the streets of Manhattan, starving - he had fainted from hunger there on the subway steps

Goleman's own shift-away reflex had been altered by an article he had recently written for The New York Times on how closing mental hospitals had converted the city's streets into psychiatric wards, and by days spent in a van with workers of a social agency that administered to the homeless

In other studies using the Good Samaritan situation, researchers find that those who do stop to help typically report that on seeing the other's distress, they felt upset too - and an empathic sense of tenderness; once one person noticed the other enough to feel empathy, the odds were very high that he would offer some help
In a study in Japan, people readily came up with accounts of kandou - times when the heart is so moved, for example by seeing a tough-looking gang member give up his seat on a train to an elderly man

assets.visual_frame_description: A rush-hour stairwell where a shirtless man lies motionless and feet step over him; one figure stops, and suddenly a circle of concern forms - food, water, a radio - while in the next frame a passerby kneels by a crumpled car and holds a woman's hand as she says 'my angel on earth.'
assets.player_mission: Play Goleman stopping on the Times Square subway steps, then the crowd that stops with him - fetch the hot dog, the bottle of water, the patrol officer's radio call - and then play the starving man who speaks only Spanish. Switch seats until you feel the shift-away reflex being reversed, and end as the 'angel on earth' who kneels by the wrecked car and holds a stranger's hand.
key_concepts: Simply paying attention allows us to build an emotional connection - lacking attention, empathy hasn't a chance

By simply stopping to take in the man's plight, Goleman seemed to snap passersby out of their urban trance and called him to their attention - as they tuned in to his predicament, they were moved to help

Urbanites learn to manage the anxiety of seeing someone in such dire straits by reflexively shifting attention away - a strategy of silent assumptions and stereotypes built from walking past the hundreds of homeless who inhabit the streets of New York and so many other modern urban centers

Psychologists use the term 'elevation' for the glow stirred by witnessing someone else's kindness - the state reported repeatedly when people tell how they felt on seeing a spontaneous act of courage, tolerance, or compassion, most commonly acts of helping the poor or sick or aiding someone in a difficult predicament

Elevation, the research suggests, may be catching: when someone sees an act of kindness, it typically stirs in them the impulse to perform one too - and psychologists speculate that hearing a story about kindness told vividly has the same emotional impact as seeing the act itself
That elevation can be contagious suggests that it travels the low road - one reason mythic tales worldwide are rife with figures who save others through their courageous deeds

On a five-day visit to Brazil with his son, the people they met seemed to get friendlier day by day: by the third day they encountered noticeably greater warmth, on the fourth day it followed them wherever they went, and by the trip's end they were hugging people good-bye at the airport

What had melted away was their own uptightness as gringos in an unfamiliar culture - like a radio set to a slightly off-channel signal, they were too preoccupied to take in the friendliness, and as they relaxed they zeroed in on the right station, the warmth that was there all along
While we are anxious or preoccupied, we fail to register the sparkle in someone's eye, the hint of a smile, or the warm tones of voice - all prime channels for sending messages of friendliness

Working memory, the amount of memory we can hold in our attention at any one moment, resides in the prefrontal cortex, the citadel of the high road - it allocates our attention by managing the backstage business of an interaction, searching memory for what to say and do even while it attends to incoming signals

Signals of worry from the amygdala flood key regions of the prefrontal cortex, manifesting as preoccupations that steal attention away from whatever else we are dealing with - distress overtaxes attention; merely being an uptight gringo will do it

A head-on collision left a woman's car crumpled like a piece of paper, with two bones broken in her right leg, and she lay pinned in the wreckage in pain and shock - a passerby she never found out his name knelt by her side, held her hand, and helped her stay calm; 'He was,' as she put it later, 'my angel on earth'

assets.visual_frame_description: A three-shelf registry labeled Know, Feel, Respond; each case arrives with its brain scan glowing - identical circuitry for self and other - while a 1909 dictionary entry for Einfühlung, 'feeling into,' is stamped at the top.
assets.player_mission: Audit every act of compassion you witness and file it under the three senses of empathy: knowing another's feelings, feeling what they feel, responding to their distress - the 1-2-3 sequence of I notice you, I feel with you, I act to help you. Record the neural evidence for each file: the shared circuitry of 'How are you feeling?' and 'How is she feeling?', the Einfühlung of the high-wire performer, the mirror-neuron richness.
key_concepts: Empathy entails some degree of emotional sharing - a prerequisite to truly understanding anyone else's inner world
Mirror neurons, as one neuroscientist puts it, are 'what give you the richness of empathy, the fundamental mechanism that makes seeing someone hurt really hurt you'

Constantin Stanislavski, the Russian developer of the famed Method for stage training, saw that an actor 'living' a part could call up his emotional memories from the past - but those memories need not be limited to our own experiences, for an actor can draw on the emotions of others through a bit of empathy
As the legendary acting coach advised, 'We must study other people and get as close to them emotionally as we can, until sympathy for them is transformed into feelings of our own'

Brain imaging studies reveal that when we answer the question 'How are you feeling?' we activate much of the same neural circuitry that lights up when we ask 'How is she feeling?' - the brain acts almost identically when we sense our own feelings and those of another

When people are asked to imitate someone's facial expression of happiness, fear, or disgust, this activates the same circuits involved when they simply observe the person, or when they spontaneously feel that emotion themselves

The German word Einfühlung, which was first rendered into English in 1909 as the newly coined word 'empathy,' more literally translates as 'feeling into' - suggesting an inner imitation of the other person's feelings

As Theodore Lipps, who imported the word 'empathy' into English, put it, 'When I observe a circus performer on a high wire, I feel I am inside him' - it's as though we experience the other person's emotions in our own body, and neuroscientists say the more active a person's mirror neuron systems, the stronger her empathy

In today's psychology, the word 'empathy' is used in three distinct senses: knowing another person's feelings; feeling what that person feels; and responding compassionately to another's distress - three varieties that seem to describe a 1-2-3 sequence: I notice you, I feel with you, and so I act to help you

Stephanie Preston and Frans de Waal - de Waal, director of Living Links at the Yerkes Primate Center, who has drawn lessons for human behavior from systematic observations of primates - argue in a major theory that in a moment of empathy both our emotions and our thoughts are primed along the same lines as those of the other person: hearing a frightened cry from someone else, we spontaneously think of what might be causing their fear

Preston has found that if someone brings to mind one of the happiest moments of her life, then imagines a similar moment from the life of one of her closest friends, the brain activates virtually the identical circuitry for these two mental acts

To understand what someone else experiences - to empathize - we utilize the same brain wiring that is active during our own experience, and mirroring occurs whenever our perception of someone automatically activates an image or felt sense in our own brain for what they are doing and expressing: what's on their mind occupies ours

assets.visual_frame_description: A great hall where three lecterns stand - Hobbes with his alms, the selfish gene with its ledger of kin, Mencius with his third-century B.C.E. maxim - while a brain scan of shared distress flickers above, a verdict pending.
assets.player_mission: Sort each explanation of altruism onto the ancient debate: Hobbes's eased pain at the beggar's misery, the selfish-gene economics of kin selection, and Mengzi's mind that cannot bear to see suffering. Rule on each with the neuroscience - the reverberating circuits, the premotor cortex preparing action - and decide which theory the hardwired empathic resonance supports.
key_concepts: Thomas Hobbes, remembered for asserting that life in our natural state is 'nasty, brutish and short,' was walking through the streets of London when he came upon an old, sickly man begging for alms - his heart touched, he immediately gave the man a generous offering

Asked by a friend if he would have done the same had there been no religious dictum or philosophical principle about helping the needy, Hobbes replied that he would, explaining that he felt some pain himself when he saw the man's misery, and just as giving alms would relieve some of the man's suffering, it 'doth also ease me'

One school of modern economic theory, following Hobbes, argues that people give to charities in part because of the pleasure they get from imagining either the relief of those they benefit or their own relief from alleviating their sympathetic distress

Latter-day versions of this theory have tried to reduce acts of altruism to disguised acts of self-interest - in one version, compassion veils a 'selfish gene' that tries to maximize its odds of being passed on by gathering obligations or by favoring the close relatives who carry it
The Chinese sage Mengzi (or Mencius) wrote in the third century B.C.E., long before Hobbes, 'All men have a mind which cannot bear to see the suffering of others'

Neuroscience now supports Mengzi's position, adding missing data to this centuries-old debate: when we see someone else in distress, similar circuits reverberate in our brain, a kind of hardwired empathic resonance that becomes the prelude to compassion

If an infant cries, her parents' brains reverberate in much the same way, which in turn automatically moves them to do something to soothe their baby's distress - our brain has been preset for kindness

We automatically go to the aid of a child who is screaming in terror, and we automatically want to hug a smiling baby - such emotional impulses are 'prepotent': they elicit reactions in us that are unpremeditated and instantaneous

Hearing an anguished scream activates the same parts of our brain that experience such anguish, as well as the premotor cortex, a sign we are preparing to act; hearing someone tell an unhappy story in doleful tones activates the listener's motor cortex as well as the amygdala and related circuits for sadness

This shared state then signals the motor area of the brain, where we prepare our response, for the relevant action - our initial perception prepares us for action: to see readies us to do, because the neural networks for perception and action share a common code in the language of the brain

Darwin, who in 1872 wrote a scholarly treatise on emotions that scientists still regard highly, saw every emotion as a predisposition to act in a unique way - fear to freeze or flee, anger to fight, joy to embrace - and brain imaging studies now show that at the neural level he was right

Emotional contagion does more than merely spread feelings - it automatically prepares the brain for appropriate action; Nature's rule of thumb holds that a biological system should use minimal energy, and the brain achieves that efficiency by firing the same neurons while both perceiving and performing an action, an economizing that repeats across brains

assets.visual_frame_description: A monkey lab where seven rhesus monkeys face chains and a shock grid glows; then a stone seminary corridor where a moaning man slumps by the doorway and forty students hurry past, the clock of urgency ticking over each head.
assets.player_mission: Face the chain-pull dilemma as one of the six rhesus monkeys: pull for food and shock the seventh in full view, or starve for five days, twelve days, rather than hurt him - and then walk the seminary corridor as one of the forty, late for your Good Samaritan sermon, past a man who is groaning. Decide in seconds, because the brain's prepotent impulse to aid is waiting to be overruled by the press of hurrying.
key_concepts: Six rhesus monkeys were trained to pull chains to get food; at one point a seventh monkey, in full view of the others, got a painful shock whenever one of them pulled for food - on seeing the pain of that shocked monkey, four of the six started pulling a different chain, one that delivered less food but inflicted no shock on the other monkey
The fifth monkey stopped pulling any chain at all for five days, and the sixth for twelve days - both starved themselves to prevent shocking the seventh monkey

A laboratory rat, suspended in the air by a harness, screeched and struggled; catching sight of the imperiled rat, one of its cagemates became upset too and managed to come to the rescue by pressing a bar that lowered the victim safely to the ground
Virtually from birth, when babies see or hear another baby crying in distress, they start crying as though they too are distressed - but they rarely cry when they hear a recording of their own cries

After about fourteen months of age, babies not only cry when they hear another baby, but they also try to relieve the other baby's suffering somehow - and the older toddlers get, the less they cry and the more they try to help

Lab rats, monkeys, and babies share an automatic impulse that rivets their attention on another's suffering, triggers similar distressed feelings in themselves, and leads them to try to help - simple: Nature conserves, preserving whatever works to use again and again

In contrast to mammals, reptiles show not the least sign of empathy, even eating their own young - and the similarity across species in sympathetic distress, coupled with the impulse to help, strongly suggests a like set of underlying circuitry in the brain

New thinking holds that our sociability has been the primary survival strategy of primate species, including our own - empathy lubricates sociability, and we humans are the social animal par excellence

On Cayo Santiago, a remote island in the Caribbean, about a thousand rhesus macaques all descend from a single band transplanted from their native India in the 1950s - when the adolescent males leave to find their place in another group, up to 20 percent of them die in fights as they try to enter an unfamiliar troupe

From spinal fluid samples of one hundred teen macaques, scientists found that the most outgoing monkeys have the lowest levels of stress hormones and stronger immune function, and are best able to approach, befriend, or challenge monkeys in the new troupe - these more sociable young monkeys are the ones most likely to survive

For wild baboons near Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, infancy holds great perils - about 10 percent of infants die in a good year, up to 35 percent in bad times - but the mothers who were most companionable, spending the most time grooming or otherwise socializing with other female baboons, had the infants most likely to survive; sociable baboons make better mothers, and the more grooming mothers give and get, the more relaxed and healthy they tend to be

In one study, the more saddened people were by the plight of a displaced orphan, the more likely they were to donate money or even offer the child a temporary place to live - regardless of how much social distance they felt; and to feel with stirs us to act for, for the preference for helping those similar to ourselves washes away when we are face-to-face with someone in agony, where the primal brain-to-brain link makes us experience their suffering as our own

chapters.title: Chapter 5: The Neuroanatomy of a Kiss

assets.visual_frame_description: A darkened neural theater where two pairs of eyes interlink their glowing orbitofrontal areas across a tea table, a clock ticking in twentieths of a second, and filaments of spindle cells arcing between the OFC and the anterior cingulate like summer lightning.
assets.player_mission: Scan a grid of social moments frozen at their critical instant - the locked gazes over tea that preceded the kiss, the professor's waiting room, the mother viewing pictures of infants, the online chat room - and ring the neural tell in each. Name whether the orbitofrontal area just assigned its like-or-dislike verdict within the one-twentieth-of-a-second window, whether spindle cells carried the snap judgment through the OFC-ACC junction, and whether the high road can still seize the microphone before the scene's verdict is stamped.
key_concepts: The eyes contain nerve projections that lead directly to a key brain structure for empathy, the orbitofrontal area (OFC) of the prefrontal cortex, so that when two people's eyes meet they have interlinked their orbitofrontal areas
The OFC sits just behind and above the orbits of the eyes, at the junction of the uppermost part of the emotional centers and the lowest part of the thinking brain

The OFC connects directly, neuron to neuron, with the cortex (the thinking brain), the amygdala (the trigger point for many emotional reactions), and the brain stem (the reptilian zones for automatic response)
In technical terms the OFC circuitry assigns 'hedonic value' to our social world, letting us know that we enjoy her, loathe them, or adore him

When mothers of newborn infants viewed pictures of their own or unfamiliar infants, fMRI showed the OFC lit up for their own babies but not the others, and the greater the OFC activity, the stronger their feelings of love and warmth

In a university study, students who spent just three to ten minutes on the first day of class getting to know a stranger rated the likely course of their relationship, and nine weeks later those first impressions predicted its actual course with remarkable accuracy

Spindle cells - brain cells shaped like a spindle with a large bulb at one end and a long, thick extension, about four times larger than other brain cells - are suspected to be the secret of the speed of social intuition and put the 'snap' in snap judgments

Spindle cells form particularly thick connections between the OFC and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), which directs our attention and coordinates thoughts, emotions, and the body's response to feelings
Spindle cells are rich in receptors for serotonin, dopamine, and vasopressin, brain chemicals that play key roles in bonding with others, love, moods, and pleasure
We humans have about a thousand times more spindle cells than our closest primate cousins, the apes, who have but a few hundred, and no other mammalian brain seems to contain spindle cells

The brain's default activity - what happens automatically when nothing much else goes on - seems to be mulling over our relationships, something like its top-rated TV show; only an impersonal task like balancing a checkbook quiets the 'people' circuits

We make judgments about people around a tenth of a second more quickly than we do about things, and in the first moment of an encounter neural areas make their initial pro-or-con judgment in just one-twentieth of a second

assets.visual_frame_description: Columbia's fMRI Research Center: a gurney sliding into the long dark tube of an MRI machine, a birdcage-like coil over the volunteer's head, a mirror at forty-five degrees reflecting the photo of a woman sobbing by a church as her sadness reshapes into wedding delight.
assets.player_mission: Play the woman studying the weeping figure by the church and talk yourself from funeral to wedding, damping the right amygdala's ultraquick verdict with an intentional reappraisal. Then switch seats and play the woman whose sister suffers attacks of anger, practicing the inner mental judo that shields you from a toxic contagion. Finally interview Kevin Ochsner about the prefrontal circuit that stirs when you view another's distress with clinical detachment rather than hope.
key_concepts: Kevin Ochsner's brain-imaging study at Columbia showed that a photo of a woman weeping by a church could be reappraised from a funeral into a wedding, replacing the first flood of negative feeling with a happier one and quieting the amygdala

The right amygdala, a trigger point for distressing emotions, makes an automatic, ultraquick emotional appraisal - a funeral - before the cortical centers for thinking have even finished analyzing the situation

The more involved the ACC, Ochsner's study suggested, the more successful the rethinking is in altering moods for the better; the greater the activity in certain prefrontal areas, the more muted the amygdala became during reappraisal
When the high road speaks up, it takes away the low road's microphone: the specific mental strategy we deploy during reappraisal determines which of several prefrontal circuits activates

One prefrontal circuit stirs when we view another person's distress in an objective, clinically detached way, as though we had no personal connection - the strategy typical of those in the health professions - while a different circuit activates when we reappraise by hoping for the best
Marcus Aurelius said millennia ago that pain 'is not due to the thing itself, but to your estimate of it, and this you have the power to revoke at any moment'
The woman whose sister becomes paranoid and adversarial practices what she calls inner mental judo: she reminds herself of the mental disorder so she does not take the anger personally

She insulates herself against the 'emotional assault' by not returning every phone call right away, scheduling less time together, and waiting a day or two after an angry voice on the answering machine

Even just naming for ourselves the emotions we feel can calm the amygdala, and the high road to choice means we are free to respond as we like even to unwanted contagion - staying cool and coming to the rescue of someone hysterical with fear
'The idea that it's all done on automatic is depressing,' Ochsner observes; 'Reappraisal alters our emotional response. When we do it intentionally, we gain conscious control of our emotions'

In Ochsner's research a volunteer lies perfectly still in the MRI wearing a birdcage-like coil that detects radio waves emitted by atoms in the brain, while a mirror at a forty-five-degree angle reflects images projected from the far end of the gurney
In Ochsner's study the women first let their initial thoughts and feelings wash through them, and only then were instructed to purposely rethink the scene in a way that would be less distressing

assets.visual_frame_description: A psychiatric intake desk at the top of an asylum stairwell, where manila folders fly open onto a wall chart of the OFC's jobs, each case stamping itself with its failure mode while a gauge labeled Emotional Brake flickers red.
assets.player_mission: Review the clinical files: the lobotomized patients, the OFC-lesion patients who hug strangers and tell bathroom jokes, the war veterans flooded by a truck backfire, the chat-room students, and the Liverpool lottery man. File each case under the OFC function that failed - impulse inhibition, regret, hedonic value, contextual appraisal, or top-down modulation of the amygdala - and stamp your verdict before the folder seals itself.
key_concepts: Prefrontal lobotomies, a psychiatric fad of the 1940s and 1950s, surgically disconnected the OFC from other brain areas, often primitively - the medical equivalent of inserting a screwdriver alongside the eyeball
While lobotomized patients' cognitive abilities remained intact, their emotions were flattened or absent altogether, and they became disoriented in social situations new to them

A man in Liverpool played the same lottery numbers - 14, 17, 22, 24, 42, and 47 - week after week, and killed himself when he saw them win the two-million-pound prize the week he had forgotten to renew his ticket
Feelings of regret stir in the OFC, yet patients with lesions in key circuits of the OFC lack all such feelings: no matter how bad their choice, they are utterly unfazed by missed opportunities

The OFC exerts a 'top-down' modulation of the amygdala, and patients with lesions in these inhibitory circuits lose the ability to suppress emotional impulses, unable for example to keep themselves from mimicking someone's scowling face

OFC-lesion patients may greet a total stranger with a hug and a kiss, make taste-less bathroom jokes, and blithely reveal embarrassing details about themselves - oblivious to the social norms they can still explain rationally

War veterans who are flooded with traumatic memories by a battle scene on the evening news or a truck backfire suffer from an overactive amygdala that sends surges of panic in mistaken reaction to cues vaguely reminiscent of the original trauma

As low-road circuitry sends up primitive impulses, the OFC evaluates them against a sophisticated reading of the moment - 'This is a library' or 'It's only our first date' - and modulates them accordingly, acting as an emotional brake

In a study where strangers were virtually paired in an online chat room, about one in five of the Internet conversations quickly became startlingly sexual, with explicit terms and outright solicitation of sex, even though the students seemed low key and polite in person

'Flaming,' in which adults make childishly offensive comments online, has been documented ever since the earliest years of the Internet because the Internet lacks the sort of feedback the OFC needs to help us stay on track socially
During in-person interactions we loop, getting an ongoing flow of feedback mainly from the person's facial expressions and tone of voice, which instantly tells us when we are on track and off

assets.visual_frame_description: A neural autobahn interchange: the low road glows hot red with mirror-neuron sparks while the high road runs cool blue beneath prefrontal towers, and at the junction an orbitofrontal switching station routes each onrushing case down its lane.
assets.player_mission: Sort a torrent of micro-events into their lane: instant primal empathy, mirror-neuron attunement, the oscillators guiding the kiss, and gut like-dislike belong to the low road; monitored attention, reappraisal, and the rational veto belong to the high road; the Ultimatum Game belongs to both at once. Justify every call with the neural evidence before the OFC switching station routes the next case.
key_concepts: The low road, with its ultrarapid mirror neuron links, operates as a sort of sixth sense, prompting us to feel with another person even though we may be only vaguely aware of our attunement
The low road triggers a sympathetic emotional state without an intervening thought - instant primal empathy
The high road opens up as we monitor a mood shift and intentionally attend to the person we're talking with, bringing our thinking brain, especially the prefrontal centers, into play
The high road adds enormous flexibility to the far more fixed and limited repertoire of the low road: as it activates, the possibilities for response increase exponentially

One stream of messages shuttles back and forth to low-road centers that spawn our initial emotional reactions, while the OFC shunts a parallel flow upward to trigger our thoughts about that reaction - the OFC is the switching station between the two roads

In the Ultimatum Game a stranger is given ten dollars to split any way you can agree; if offered two dollars most people become indignant and, if offered just one, outraged, though taking it seems perfectly reasonable to any economist

People will sometimes be willing to sacrifice up to a month's salary just to punish an unfair offer; with only one round, lowball offers often result in anger, but with multiple rounds the two players are more likely to reach a satisfactory bargain
Jonathan Cohen, director of the Center for the Study of Brain, Mind, and Behavior at Princeton University, pioneered 'neuro-economics,' scanning partners who play the Ultimatum Game

The more powerful the low road's reactivity - in this case the insula, which can react during certain emotions as strongly as the amygdala - the less rational the players' reactions from the economic perspective, while the more active the prefrontal area, the more balanced the outcome

In his essay 'The Vulcanization of the Brain,' a reference to Star Trek's hyperrational Mr. Spock, Cohen contrasts high-road deliberative processing of valenced information with low-road emotions and predispositions to act rashly

Over the course of human brain development, the size of the prefrontal cortex has largely been what set us apart from other primates, which have much smaller prefrontal areas; the prefrontal cortex wields the power to say no to impulse

The low road's initial like-or-dislike decision registers firmly in the OFC, which then guides neural activity there for another fifth of a second while nearby prefrontal areas offer up information about social context

assets.visual_frame_description: A panoramic social brain under siege: the OFC switching station battles an inflamed amygdala while spindle-cell lines crackle overhead, and behind it a classroom where a boy's face flushes crimson while a countdown clock ticks in twentieths of a second.
assets.player_mission: Stand inside Jonathan Cohen's scanner and play the Ultimatum Game against a one-dollar offer, winning a fair bargain without letting the insula's 'go to hell' rashness take the wheel - then refuse the second round of molten chocolate mousse. Survive the war-veteran flashback and the online chat room, and finish by reengineering the low road: take David Guy back into the classroom, expose the traffic officer to her trigger phrase, and reconsolidate a fear memory with a new perspective so the amygdala loses its conditioning.
key_concepts: Joseph LeDoux, who has studied the amygdala for decades at the Center for Neural Science at New York University, likes to call it the brain's 'Fear Central'

David Guy was sixteen when his stage fright began in English class; his classmates' sarcasm was merciless, and merely imagining their scorn was enough to activate his amygdala and flood his body with stress hormones

Social phobia, as the psychiatric diagnostic manual dubs these anxieties, is the most common of all phobias, claimed by one in five Americans, and takes forms from meeting new people to eating in public or using a shared restroom

Our memories are in part reconstructions: retrieving a memory reconsolidates it, slightly altered chemically by a new protein synthesis, so the next time we retrieve it, it comes up as we last modified it

If at the time of fear we tell ourselves something that eases its grip, the memory is reencoded with less power over us, and LeDoux says the cells in our amygdala can reprogram so that we lose the original fear conditioning

Exposure sessions begin with getting the person relaxed, often through a few minutes of slow abdominal breathing, then confront the threatening situation in a careful gradation culminating in the very worst version

In her exposure therapy, the New York City traffic officer had the phrase 'low-life bitch' repeated first in a flat tone, then with increasing emotional intensity, and finally with added obscene gestures, until she could stay relaxed

One cognitive therapist uses therapy groups as a trial audience for patients overcoming the fear of speaking in public, coaching the group to act in ways that will be difficult for the patient, from snide comments to looking bored or disapproving
Says LeDoux, 'It's something like what happens naturally when we churn a worry over in our mind, and come to a new perspective' - we use the high road to reengineer the low

If the first guy offers just one dollar, says Cohen, the other's response might well be 'Go to hell,' a result that drives economists crazy because their theories assume people will always try to maximize their rewards

The phrase 'the social brain' does not refer to a phrenology bump or some specific brain nodule but to the particular set of circuitry orchestrated as people relate to each other, and no major zone appears to be exclusively devoted to social life

The brain's 100 billion neurons with their roughly 100 trillion interconnections are organized into modules that behave something like an intricate swinging mobile, where activity in any one part can reverberate through the whole system

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The PONS Signal Sweep
assets.visual_frame_description: A video editing bay running PONS-style clips in a loop, a waveform of the voice's tone and a face grid frozen mid-flicker, with a scoreboard that grades each guess against Robert Rosenthal's norms.
assets.player_mission: Scan two-second snippets from Judith Hall's videotapes - returning a faulty item to a store, talking about the death of a friend - and name the emotion leaking from face, body, or voice before the clip ends. Then sweep the embassy interview, the middle-school soccer field, and the dinner party, and ring which channel carried the tell: the flicker of disgust, the sarcastic taunt defused, or the insult disguised as wit.
key_concepts: The chubby twelve-year-old artist defused a sarcastic taunt on the way to soccer with 'Yeah, I'm going to try - but I'm not very good at it,' adding 'I'm great at art,' until his antagonist offered, 'Maybe I can show you a few things about how to play'

By keeping cool, the aspiring artist resisted the pull to anger in an invisible tug-of-war between the boys' brains - a display of neural jujitsu that transformed their shared emotional chemistry from a hostile range to a positive one

Edward Thorndike, the Columbia University psychologist, first proposed social intelligence in a 1920 article in Harper's Monthly Magazine, observing it 'shows itself abundantly in the nursery, on the playground, in barracks and factories and salesrooms' but eludes the formal standardized conditions of the testing laboratory
'The best mechanic in a factory may fail as a foreman for lack of social intelligence,' Thorndike wrote, noting such interpersonal effectiveness was vital for leadership
By the late 1950s David Wechsler, creator of one of the most widely used measures of IQ, dismissed social intelligence as merely 'general intelligence applied to social situations'

Richard Davidson, director of the Laboratory for Affective Neuroscience at the University of Wisconsin, observes, 'All emotions are social. You can't separate the cause of an emotion from the world of relationships - our social interactions are what drive our emotions'

The embassy applicant's momentary look of disgust, spotted by an interviewer who then consulted an Interpol data bank and found a fugitive wanted by police in several countries, demonstrates primal empathy - a low-road capacity largely activated by mirror neurons
'Even though we can stop talking, we cannot stop sending signals' about what we feel, so 'when it comes to emotions, we cannot not communicate'

The Profile of Nonverbal Sensitivity (PONS), made by Judith Hall and Dane Archer as students of Robert Rosenthal, asks people to guess what's going on emotionally from a two-second snippet of a scene, such as Hall's face or body alone or just her voice

Those who do well on the PONS are rated as more interpersonally sensitive, get higher job performance ratings, and are liked more; women score about three percent higher on average, and nearly everyone improves from early adolescence into their mid-twenties

Simon Baron-Cohen's Reading the Mind in the Eyes test, designed with his research group at Cambridge University, presents thirty-six images of eyes; high scorers are gifted at empathy, while those who do poorly in the extreme are likely to have autism

Paul Ekman's MicroExpression Training Tool flashes seven expressions - sadness, anger, fear, surprise, disgust, contempt, or happiness - in just a fifteenth of a second, and most people jump from around 40 to 50 percent correct to 80 to 90 percent after about twenty minutes of training

assets.visual_frame_description: A university waiting room where two strangers on a couch are secretly watched through a camera concealed in a closet; a conversation meter tracks who first asks a question about the other, and an embassy desk with an Interpol screen glows in the background.
assets.player_mission: Sit as the top-performing salesperson who first listens and understands a client's needs before matching anything you have to them - and take the client's side in a justified complaint against your own company. Then swap seats with William Ickes's hidden-camera volunteers and write down what you thought your partner was thinking at key points of the six-minute wait. Finish by interviewing the visa applicant face to face and deciding whether his story holds.
key_concepts: Attunement is attention that goes beyond momentary empathy to a full, sustained presence that facilitates rapport: we offer a person our total attention, listen fully, and seek to understand the other person rather than just making our own point
'Talking at a person rather than listening to him reduces a conversation to a monologue' - when I hijack a conversation by talking at you, I'm fulfilling my needs without considering yours

Top-performing salespeople and client managers do not approach a customer with the determination to make a sale; they see themselves as consultants who first listen and understand the client's needs, and they will even take a client's side in a justified complaint about their own company

Deep listening numbers among the top three abilities of those in the helping professions whose work has been rated outstanding by their organizations, and listening well distinguishes the best managers, teachers, and leaders

The Harvard Business Review notes that 'a five-minute conversation can be a perfectly meaningful human moment' if you set aside what you are doing, put down the memo, disengage from your laptop, and focus on the person you're with

William Ickes, the University of Texas psychologist who pioneered research on empathic accuracy, says it distinguishes 'the most tactful advisors, the most diplomatic officials, the most effective negotiators, the most electable politicians, the most productive salespersons, the most successful teachers, and the most insightful therapists'

In Ickes's hidden-camera method, two volunteers who think they are merely waiting are secretly videotaped from a closet, then each watches the six-minute tape and writes down their own thoughts and feelings and what they suspect the other was thinking and feeling

In that experiment one woman felt silly because she couldn't remember a teacher's name and her partner accurately guessed 'she was maybe feeling sort of odd,' while another woman idly recalled a stage play and her male partner guessed, 'She was wondering if I would ask her out'

Couples who are more accurate in reading each other during the first year or two of marriage have higher levels of satisfaction and are more likely to last; a partner who realizes the other feels bad but has no clue what's on their mind signals a rockier relationship

Conscious awareness of someone's intentions allows for more accurate empathy, and a more explicit understanding of underlying motives can mean the difference between life and death face to face with a mugger or an angry crowd

Mirror neurons attune us to what someone intends to do, but at a subliminal level, which is why the cognitive steps of empathic accuracy - engaging the neocortex, particularly the prefrontal area - bring high-road circuitry to the primal empathy of the low

Intentionally paying more attention to someone may be the best way to encourage the emergence of rapport, orienting our neural circuits for connectivity and maximizing the likelihood that synchrony and positive feelings might bloom

credibility.basis: Goleman popularizes social-neuroscience research but overreaches on mirror neurons, 'social intelligence' as a measurable trait, and deterministic brain claims, drawing sharp cr...

assets.visual_frame_description: A psychology department ledger with two great columns, Awareness and Facility, where case cards drop into their domain while a low-road/high-road gauge shows where each ability lives in the brain.
assets.player_mission: Audit a week of case files and file each encounter under one of the eight domains - primal empathy, attunement, empathic accuracy, social cognition, synchrony, self-presentation, influence, and concern. Stamp each entry with its neural lane: pure low road for synchrony and primal empathy, mingled high and low for empathic accuracy and influence, and flag every dyssemic case with its cause: failed learning, emotional trauma, or a diagnosable neurological disorder.
key_concepts: The ingredients of social intelligence organize into two broad categories: social awareness, what we sense about others, and social facility, what we then do with that awareness

Social awareness spans primal empathy (feeling with others, sensing nonverbal emotional signals), attunement (listening with full receptivity), empathic accuracy (understanding another's thoughts, feelings, and intentions), and social cognition (knowing how the social world works)

Social facility spans synchrony (interacting smoothly at the nonverbal level), self-presentation (presenting ourselves effectively), influence (shaping the outcome of social interactions), and concern (caring about others' needs and acting accordingly)
Synchrony and primal empathy are purely low-road capacities, while empathic accuracy and influence mingle high and low

Social cognition includes knowing what's expected in most any social situation, from the manners appropriate in a five-star restaurant to decoding who might be the most powerful person in a group, and its chronic failure complicates psychological difficulties ranging from depression to schizophrenia

The social cognition school, which reduces social intelligence to general intelligence applied to the social world, ignores what we actually do while interacting - a rather blatant failing, since someone bright at social cognition but lacking social facility will still be painfully awkward with people

Dyssemia is a deficit in reading - and so acting on - the nonverbal signs that guide smooth interactions: dyssemic children may fail to look at people speaking to them, stand too close, show facial expressions inappropriate to their emotional state, or seem tactless

An estimated 85 percent of those with dyssemia failed to learn how to read or respond to nonverbal signals, another 10 percent or so had an emotional trauma short-circuit the learning, and only about 5 percent have a diagnosable neurological disorder

Remedial programs for dyssemia teach the nonverbal ingredients of synchrony - gestures and posture, the use of touch, eye contact, tone of voice, and pacing - until people 'overlearn' the more harmonious responses so they come spontaneously

The ability to 'control and mask' emotional expression is key to self-presentation: society's norms tacitly approve a woman crying openly but frown on men shedding tears, while a powerful woman is expected to display anger when a group's goal has been frustrated - alpha women meet the entrance requirement

Influence combines self-control (modulating an aggressive impulse) with empathy (reading the other person to gauge what the least force necessary might be) and social cognition (recognizing the operative norms in a situation)

A study of charitable giving done in the Netherlands found that a person's sense of social concern predicted the likelihood that they would donate to the needy, and concern at work translates into good organizational citizenship

credibility.basis: Goleman popularizes social-neuroscience research but overreaches on mirror neurons, 'social intelligence' as a measurable trait, and deterministic brain claims, drawing sharp cr...

assets.visual_frame_description: A sorting carousel with eight bins arranged around a map of the social brain; vignettes fly in like film stills, and a caption above the racks reads 'Simply sensing how another feels does not guarantee fruitful interactions.'
assets.player_mission: Sort a parade of vignettes into the bin that owns them: the embassy interviewer and the PONS high scorers into the awareness bins; the Reagan microphone grab, the traffic officer, and the Good Samaritan seminarians into the facility bins. Justify each call with the evidence on the card, and reject any case where sensing another's feelings was never turned into action.
key_concepts: In 1980, when Ronald Reagan was running for the Republican presidential nomination, he grabbed another microphone after the moderator cut him off and declared in angry tones, 'I paid for this show. I'm paying for this microphone,' a moment later confessed by a campaign adviser to have been planned

Charisma is one aspect of self-presentation: charismatic speakers can 'play' an audience, using timing and rhythmic cadence to entrain the crowd's emotions, becoming senders of emotion while the audience is the recipient of the contagion

A college student with animated energy and exuberant expressivity was well liked by her peers but had gaps in self-control, gasping with delight or making sounds of disgust throughout her professor's lecture until a few times she had to leave the room

In the Good Samaritan study the seminary students rushing to deliver practice sermons heard the moans of the man in the doorway they had to pass; those who stopped to help exhibited concern, because 'empathy alone matters little if we fail to act'
When women watched videotapes of a baby crying, those who most strongly 'caught' the baby's sadness showed the biggest frowns and had the strongest desire to pick him up and hold him

One longitudinal study found that five-to-seven-year-olds who were least upset on seeing their own mother's distress were most likely to be 'antisocial' as adults, suggesting that fostering young children's attention to and concern for others may prevent later misbehavior

Bill and Melinda Gates deploy the best practices of the business world against the devastating health problems of the world's poor, and they spend time meeting the people they help - mothers in Mozambique, victims of AIDS in India - which primes their empathy

Manipulative people can be skilled in other abilities of social intelligence, but they fail at concern, so a deficiency in this aspect of social facility should most strongly identify antisocial types
Certain New York traffic cops who use the least-force approach report the fewest incidents with angry motorists that escalate into violence

The very best police officers are adept at exercising influence - constructively shaping the outcome of an interaction with tact and self-control - using the least force necessary while perhaps making a strong show of force to back it up

It can be counterproductive to signal your empathic accuracy by saying 'I don't turn you on' or 'You don't love me!': absorbing such an insight and acting on it tacitly is more prudent, and the muted tones that are best for Beijing will seem too understated in Guadalajara

The varieties of social intelligence are no substitute for other kinds of expertise: as one businessman said of another, 'He's got that ability to make people like him. But you couldn't pick a worse person - he's got no follow-up tech skills'

credibility.basis: Goleman popularizes social-neuroscience research but overreaches on mirror neurons, 'social intelligence' as a measurable trait, and deterministic brain claims, drawing sharp cr...

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Good Samaritan Corridor
assets.visual_frame_description: A seminary corridor at dusk with a slumped figure in a doorway; overhead the four icons of awareness feed the four icons of facility, and a final gauge ticks between Empathy and Action as the practice-sermon bell rings.
assets.player_mission: Run the full four-and-four gauntlet: read the fugitive's microexpression, attune as the consultant, decode the marriage data, and file the organizational politics - then walk the corridor of the Good Samaritan study and hear the moans in the doorway. Pass or fail the concern gate, where empathy alone matters little if you fail to act, and close with Ekman's post-test, aiming for the 80 to 90 percent range on your final score.
key_concepts: Goleman scored a respectable 86 percent on Ekman's post-test, up from 50 percent on the pretest, finding that when he trusted his gut he was more often right, while when he explained the blur rationally he was usually wrong

People trained in Ekman's method become more adept at detecting real-life microexpressions, like the look of abject sadness that flitted across British spy Kim Philby's face in his last public interview before he fled to the Soviet Union, or the hint of disgust zipping by as Kato Kaelin testified at the O. J. Simpson murder trial

'The low road is eminently trainable. But why haven't we learned this already? Because we've never gotten the right feedback before,' Ekman told Goleman, who advises, 'You want to overlearn this skill'

Microexpressions are emotional signals that flit across the face in less than a third of a second; while a single discrepant microexpression does not inevitably indicate that the person is lying, outright falsehoods usually involve this sort of emotional deceptiveness

Ekman's training bypasses the high road and connects directly to the low, contradicting the assumption of most psychologists that such rapid, automatic, and spontaneous behavior was largely beyond our ability to improve

In the amnesia tale told by Joseph LeDoux, the woman's temporal lobe lesions - part of the high-road circuitry - left her unable to recognize the doctor who pricked her with a hidden tack, but her intact amygdala meant that though she did not recognize him, she knew not to trust him

The social architecture of the brain intertwines the high and low roads, which work in parallel as necessary rudders in the social world; conventional ideas of social intelligence have too often focused on high-road talents like extracting the rules, protocols, and norms that guide appropriate behavior

Goleman stands with the late Lawrence Kohlberg, who argued that eliminating human values from social intelligence impoverishes the concept, devolving it into the pragmatics of influence and control
When Thorndike originally proposed measuring social intelligence in the 1920s, next to nothing was known about the neural basis of IQ, let alone about interpersonal skill

The women who most strongly caught the baby's sadness on videotape not only mirrored its physiology but had the strongest desire to pick him up and hold him - the more we empathize with someone in need and feel concern, the greater our urge to help

Concern is the impulse that lies at the root of the helping professions - medicine and social work are in a sense their public embodiment - and those who work in them thrive when this capacity waxes but burn out when it wanes

assets.visual_frame_description: A café where two silhouettes either fuse into a single glowing loop or slide apart into one light and one shadow; above the table a gauge swings between Buber's two poles while the Japanese word amae glows softly.
assets.player_mission: Scan a sequence of everyday encounters - the sympathy call with the clicking keyboard, the speed-dating monologue, the ice cream offer, the hospital morning rounds - and ring the mode: I-You or I-It. Judge whether attunement is present or absent, whether the other person feels felt or merely hollow, and stamp each scene before the telephone clicks again.
key_concepts: In the sympathy call, the woman could hear the clicking of computer keys as her friend answered his e-mail while she described her sister's long illness, and his comments became increasingly hollow, perfunctory, and off-point - a 'gut punch' of what Martin Buber called I-It
Buber coined the term I-It for the range of relations running from merely detached to utterly exploitative, in which others become objects and we treat someone more as a thing than as a person

Psychologists use the term 'agentic' for the cold approach that views people solely as instruments to be used toward our own goals: I am agentic when I care not at all about your feelings but only about what I want from you

Agency contrasts with 'communion,' a state of high mutual empathy where your feelings do more than matter to me - they change me; while we are in communion we stay in synch, meshed in a mutual feedback loop
When we multitask - that common addiction of modern life - and talking gets added to the mix, we readily slide into the It mode

Opera singer Allison Charney employed a 'dating test' when she was single: she counted how long it took before her date asked a question with the word 'you' in it, and on her first date with Adam Epstein, the man she married a year later, she didn't even have time to start the clock

Buber described I-You (or 'I and Thou,' as the phrase entered American popular culture) in his 1937 book on a philosophy of relationships as a special bond, an attuned closeness often found between husbands and wives, family members, and good friends

In German, the form of 'you' that Buber used - Du - is the most intimate, the word friends and lovers use with each other, and for Buber the human relationship with the divine is the one I-You connection that can be indefinitely sustained

In the I-It mode we treat other people as means to some other end, while in the I-You mode our relationship with them becomes an end in itself; the boundary is porous and fluid - every You will sometimes become an It, and every It has the potential for becoming a You

A defining quality of I-You engagement is 'feeling felt,' the distinct sensation when someone has become the target of true empathy - we sense that the other person knows how we feel, and so we feel known
Carl Rogers proposed that therapeutic empathy is achieved when the therapist attunes to the client to a point where the client feels understood - feels known as a You
Psychoanalysts use the somewhat cumbersome term 'intersubjectivity' for the meshing of two people's inner worlds, which the phrase 'I-you' describes more lyrically

assets.visual_frame_description: A living room with a bowl of ice cream on the table and two people circling an unasked question; behind them the white coats of a hospital gather around a bed as the scene dissolves into the morning after surgery.
assets.player_mission: Play Takeo Doi in the American living room and decline the ice cream you are actually hungry for, then play the host who senses what is unspoken and presses the offer a second time. Swap seats with the woman on the sympathy call and then with her friend who must choose between his e-mail and her hour of pain, and finish by giving Mary Duffy the single small gesture of personhood she was denied at morning rounds.
key_concepts: Takeo Doi, a Japanese psychiatrist on his first visit to America, could not bring himself to admit his hunger when a host asked point-blank, and he was disappointed to hear his host say 'I see' and drop the offer of the ice cream

In Japan, Doi notes, a host would simply have sensed his hunger and given him something to eat without having to ask if he wanted it - that sensing of another's needs bespeaks the high value placed on the I-You mode in Japanese culture
The Japanese word amae refers to empathy that is taken for granted, and acted upon, without calling attention to itself; in the orbit of amae we feel felt

Doi sees the warm connectedness of the mother-infant relationship - in which the mother intuitively senses what the baby needs - as the prototype of this heightened attunement, extending into every close social tie in Japanese daily life
English has no word for amae, whose unvoiced attitude is something like: if I feel it, so should you - and so I needn't tell you what I want, feel, or need

The stronger our relationship with someone, the more open and attentive to them we are likely to be; the more personal history we have shared, the more readily we will sense how they feel and the more similarly we will think about and react to whatever may arise

Emmanuel Lévinas observes that I-It implies the most superficial of relationships - thinking about the other person rather than attuning to her: I-It stays on the surface, while I-You plunges into the depths

Freud saw that whatever establishes significant points in common between people arouses 'fellow feelings,' and that beneath this surface connection intense looping could forge outright identification - a sense that the other and oneself are virtually one and the same
Husbands and wives tend to find it easier to name ways they are similar to each other than ways they differ - but only if they are happy with each other; if not, the differences loom larger

We commonly hold an overly optimistic 'illusion of invulnerability,' estimating the odds that we or our loved ones will fall prey to cancer or an auto accident as much lower than the odds we estimate for other people
Two tightly looped people mesh minds, even smoothly finishing sentences for each other - a sign of a vibrant relationship that marital researchers call 'high-intensity validation'

Mary Duffy, who had realized she had ceased being known as a person and was now simply 'the carcinoma in Room B-2,' was stripped of her nightgown by a doctor lecturing medical students who asked distractedly, 'Have you passed gas yet?'; her comeback, 'No, I don't do that until the third date,' only offended him

assets.visual_frame_description: A row of office doors - journalist, surgeon, officer, waiter, therapist - each with a clipboard; a ledger balances detachment against the empathy needed for rapport while Sartre's 'dance of the grocer' plays on a screen.
assets.player_mission: Audit professional encounters against the principle of professional distance: the journalist's code in Cambodia, the surgeon's operating rule, the police officer's impartiality, the waiter's role, and the therapist's first session. Flag each file where detachment goes so far that no I-You feeling can bloom, and balance the ledger with the studies showing where rapport is essential - the working alliance, the patient's compliance.
key_concepts: Nicholas Kristof, the Pulitzer Prize-winning New York Times columnist, did 'something dreadfully unjournalistic' in Cambodia: he bought a tiny, quivering teenage girl named Srey Neth from a pimp for $150 and helped set her and another girl free

A year later Srey Neth finished at a beauty school in Phnom Penh and was looking forward to starting her own shop, while the other girl was drifting back to the easy money; Kristof's columns moved readers to send donations to a charity that helped her restart her life

The journalist's code is a mandate for an I-It relationship, much like the codes held by other professionals from doctors to police officers: a surgeon should not operate on someone with whom she has a strong personal relationship, lest her feelings interfere with her mental clarity

Maintaining professional distance means seeing a person in terms of their role - patient, criminal - without attuning to the person within the role; while the low road connects us instantly to the other person's distress, prefrontal systems can increase our emotional separation enough so we can think more clearly

The It mode has decided advantages for daily life: implicit social rules guide us in deciding which people we need not loop with, so the waitress or store clerk is treated as a one-dimensional It, ignoring the 'rest' of them

Jean-Paul Sartre described public roles as a 'ceremony' of sorts: 'There is the dance of the grocer, of the tailor, of the auctioneer, by which they endeavor to persuade their clientele that they are nothing but a grocer, a tailor, an auctioneer'

A waiter's dignified aloofness spares him intrusions into his private life and at the same time creates a sphere of privacy for the diners he serves, giving him a bubble of privacy even in public life

Studies of people interacting with those in a formal helping role - physician, nurse, counselor, psychotherapist - show that the standard ingredients of rapport there are notably weaker on both sides than between people in informal encounters

In psychotherapy the interpersonal chemistry between therapist and client determines whether a working alliance will form, and in medicine a good rapport helps the patient trust the physician sufficiently to comply with his recommendations

Projection ignores the other person's inner reality: when we are projecting, we assume the other feels and thinks as we do - a tendency noted by David Hume, who observed a 'remarkable inclination' in human nature to bestow on other people 'the same emotions we observe in ourselves'

The psychoanalyst who felt subtly nervous at his new patient's crisply creased, wrinkle-free pants - 'the main Eddie Bauer catalog entry, and I was the addendum on the back page' - later recalled his own mother's repeated exhortations to wear pressed slacks
The analyst's challenge is to distinguish his own projections - technically the 'countertransference' - from genuine empathy; if projection makes the other an It, empathy sees the other as a You

assets.visual_frame_description: Twin shelves labeled It and You flank a porous gate where the two modes bleed into each other; each interaction hologram must be filed, with a third bin marked 'Every You will sometimes become an It' standing at the threshold.
assets.player_mission: Sort a stream of interactions - the e-mail condolence call, the speed-dating brother, the ice cream offer, the medical rounds, Kristof's purchase, the waiter, the therapist's session - into It, You, or the fluid boundary between them. The high road, with its facility in rationality and cognition, may suffice for the It, but the You, where we attune, engages the low road
When we expect to be treated as a You, the It treatment feels terrible, as happened on that hollow phone call; in such moments You shrivels into It
Empathy opens the door to I-You relations - we respond not just from the surface but with a wider swath; as Buber put it, I-You 'can only be spoken with the whole being'
We are inevitably troubled when someone we expect to loop with fails to take up their half of the circuit, and we feel bereft - something like a baby whose mother refuses to pay attention to her

When we meet someone in a professional role we tend to focus on a need or on some desired outcome, whereas with casual acquaintances our rapport heightens to the degree that we both engage in a nonverbal dance of mutual attention, smiling, coordinating posture and movement
Buber is passé in philosophical circles these days, but the French philosopher Emmanuel Lévinas has largely filled his role as a commentator on relationships

As we grow to identify with each other, the mind's categories undergo a merging of sorts, so that we unconsciously think about those most important to us in very much the same ways we think about ourselves
'Feeling felt' is the distinct sensation of being known - the unvoiced attitude of amae being that if I feel it, so should you, and so I needn't tell you what I want, feel, or need

Ordinary life inevitably swings between the two modes: we have a sort of divided self, two 'tidily circled-off provinces,' one It and one You, and we handle the details of life in the It mode through utilitarian communications focused on getting things done
The person in the It role always has an option to attend to someone as a You, temporarily stepping into full personhood

assets.visual_frame_description: The UCLA fMRI map of the anterior cingulate cortex flaring like a fire alarm; around it a savanna night where a band huddles at a fire and a lone figure walks away into the dark, while in the foreground a hospital bed stands stripped of its blanket.
assets.player_mission: Hold the line at the neural alarm: when Mary Duffy is stripped of her personhood at morning rounds, supply the I-You gesture that affirms her dignity, and when the mother hears her baby cry, respond before the ACC stops burning. Walk the prehistory of the band where banishment was a death sentence, face the e-mail-typing friend and decide whether to loop, and defeat the social pain that registers in the same brain area as physical hurt.
key_concepts: Our brain registers social rejections in the very area that activates when we are hurt physically: the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), which is known to generate, among other things, the distressing sensations of bodily pain

Matthew Lieberman and Naomi Eisenberger of UCLA suggest that the ACC operates as a neural alarm system for detecting the danger of rejection and for alerting other parts of the brain to react accordingly
The ACC, Lieberman and Eisenberger propose, forms part of a 'social attachment system' that piggybacks on the existing wiring for alerting the brain to physical harm
In human prehistory being part of a band was essential for survival; exclusion could be a death sentence, as is still true today for infant mammals in the wild

The very metaphors we use - a 'broken heart' and 'hurt feelings' - indicate the physical nature of the emotional ache, and the words that describe social pain in many languages borrow from the lexicon of physical hurts

A monkey infant whose ACC is damaged will fail to cry in distress when separated from its mother; a monkey mother whose ACC has lesions no longer responds to the cries of a distressed infant by gathering it close for protection
When a human mother hears her baby cry, her ACC lights up with activity until she responds

Tears and laughter share proximity in the brain stem, the oldest part of the brain, and come spontaneously in primal moments of social connection - births and deaths, weddings and long-deferred reunions

Psychologists have coined the term 'social depression' for the particular unhappiness caused by troubled, threatened relationships, and social rejection - or fearing it - is one of the most common causes of anxiety
Feelings of inclusion depend not so much on having frequent social contacts or numerous relationships as on how accepted we feel, even in just a few key relationships
When we hope to be a You, being treated like an It, as though we do not matter, carries a particularly harsh sting

Our yearning for connection is a primal human need, minimally for a cushion for survival; its neural echo heightens our sensitivity to the difference between It and You and makes us feel social rejection as deeply as physical pain - which is why those who always regard others as It are particularly disturbing

assets.visual_frame_description: A prison visiting room where a calm voice says 'I had to turn that part of me off'; a tri-partite scanner labels each passing face Narcissist, Mach, or Psychopath while the shared core - social malevolence, self-centeredness, emotional coldness - glows beneath all three.
assets.player_mission: Scan a sequence of scenes - the strangler's prison answer, Andre on the practice field, the European manager's office, Peter in the therapy group, the erotic-reading experiment - and ring the triad type: narcissist, Mach, or psychopath. Call the tell: the turned-off part, the tunnel-vision empathy, or the total absence of anticipatory fear, and stamp each scene before it dissolves.
key_concepts: Leonard Wolf's real-life serial killer, who had murdered ten people including three of his own family members and strangled his victims, answered the question 'Didn't you feel any pity for them?' with 'Oh, no - I had to turn that part of me off. If I had felt any of their distress, I couldn't have done it'
Empathy is the prime inhibitor of human cruelty: withholding our natural inclination to feel with another allows us to treat the other as an It, and suppressing that inclination unleashes cruelty

The Dark Triad - narcissists, Machiavellians, and psychopaths - share to varying degrees an unappealing, though sometimes well-concealed, core: social malevolence and duplicity, self-centeredness and aggression, and emotional coldness

Most people who fall into the Dark Triad do not qualify for a psychiatric diagnosis; the far more common 'subclinical' variety live among us, populating offices, schools, bars, and the routine byways of daily life

Andre, the football player with a reputation as 'flashy,' is chronically late to practice, struts 'like he's God's gift to football,' never throws a decent block for another player, and nearly got into a fight with a teammate who passed to a scoring player instead of him

Narcissists are driven by one motive - dreams of glory - and, though bored by routine, flourish when facing a difficult challenge, a trait adaptive in domains from litigation to leadership where performance under stress counts

Michael Maccoby, a psychoanalyst who has studied and treated narcissistic leaders, observes that the type has become increasingly common at the top echelons of business as competitive tensions - as well as executive pay and glamour - have escalated
Whether a given narcissist is healthy or unhealthy can be gauged by their capacity for empathy: the more impaired the person's ability to consider others, the less healthy is their narcissism

Unhealthy narcissists crave to be admired more than to be loved, can close or sell a company or lay off multitudes without an ounce of sympathy, and avoid even constructive feedback, which they perceive as an attack

One narcissistic CEO who flew into rages at helpful suggestions traced his anger to childhood feelings of being unappreciated by his aloof father, and sought emotional restitution in the form of unstinting praise - until insight let him learn to laugh at his craving for applause

The slogan of the narcissist might be 'Others exist to adore me,' and among the Dark Triad narcissists alone are blatant in their self-inflation and braggadocio, with a bias that takes credit for successes but never blame for failure

In the erotic-reading experiment, played out 120 times each with a different man, most men forgave the flustered woman - especially hearing she needed the money for tuition - but those with narcissistic tendencies were outraged by the slights, retaliated most, and on a test of attitudes approved most of coercive tactics
