assets.visual_frame_description: A prison visiting room with a thick glass partition between two chairs; a management office where a charming face and a petty tyrant alternate on the same body; a therapist's couch where a man learns to laugh at his craving for applause.
assets.player_mission: Interview the strangler across the prison table as Leonard Wolf, and press the question he asked: 'How could you do such a terrible thing to people?' Then play the narcissistic CEO's therapy session and trace his rages to the aloof father, and finally the consultant evaluating the charming European manager. Extract the tell in each voice - the turned-off part, the craving for applause, the split reputation - and judge the empathy deficit before the session ends.
key_concepts: The narcissistic CEO, once aware of his pattern, announced to his top team that he was in psychoanalysis and asked what they thought; after a long pause one executive said he didn't seem as angry anymore, 'so whatever he was doing, he should keep it up'

The manager at the European industrial giant was feared and loathed by the people working for him but utterly charming to his boss; when the consultant recommended his replacement, he found another high-level job immediately because he made such a good first impression

When Niccolò Machiavelli wrote The Prince, the sixteenth-century manual for seizing and holding political power through cunning manipulation, he took for granted that the aspiring ruler had only his own interests at heart, caring not at all about the people he ruled or crushed

The first test for Machs was actually based on statements from Machiavelli's books, like 'The biggest difference between most criminals and other people is that the criminals are stupid enough to get caught'

Machs, like narcissists, see others in strictly utilitarian terms - as an It to manipulate for their own ends; one confided to a counselor that he had just 'fired' his girlfriend, seeing people as interchangeable parts, one as good as another

Far more than the narcissist or psychopath, the Mach remains realistic about himself and others, neither making inflated claims nor striving to impress - he prefers to see things clearly, all the better to exploit them

Machs typically have tunnel-vision empathy: they can bring someone's emotions into focus mainly when they wish to use that person for their own ends, and otherwise are generally poorer at empathic attunement than others

The coldness of the Mach stems from a core deficit in processing emotions - both in themselves and in others - so at a moment of unease they may not know whether they are feeling 'sad, tired, hungry or ill'

While the Mach's head knows what to do, his heart remains clueless: their shrewd social cognition notes nuances and figures out how people might react, and these abilities allow their legendary social slickness

Some evolutionary theorists argue that human intelligence first emerged as crafty operation in the service of one's own interests: in mankind's earliest eras, victory lay in displaying just enough deviousness to get a lion's share without getting booted out of the group

A Mach's personal history inevitably will be littered with resentful ex-friends, ex-lovers, and ex-business associates, though a highly mobile society may offer a receptive ecological niche where their misdeeds never catch up with them
Every totalitarian ruler, for instance, justifies his own tyranny as needed to protect the state from some sinister enemy, even if only a concocted one

assets.visual_frame_description: A hospital intake office where a court order sits on the desk; a polygraph trace shows flat lines where sweating and heart rate should spike as a shock approaches, and a ledger of childhood warning signs runs down the wall.
assets.player_mission: Review the intake files: Peter's criminal history, the electric-shock waiting experiments, the brain-imaging study of criminal psychopaths, the 'successful psychopaths,' and the childhood warning signs. Classify each case against the hallmarks - deceit and reckless disregard, no remorse, no anticipatory fear - and stamp the diagnosis before the court order seals the file.
key_concepts: Peter, in the hospital by court order after violating parole, took from the cafeteria discussion only the thought of how much money was in the cash register, how many staff were between him and the exit, and how far he would have to get before he could find a chick and have a good time

Peter's diagnosis was that of psychopath, or 'antisocial personality disorder' as the psychiatric diagnostic manual labels it ('sociopath' has also had its vogue), whose hallmarks are deceit and a reckless disregard for others

A psychopath's consistent irresponsibility begets no remorse - only indifference to the emotional pain others may suffer; Peter found utterly foreign the idea that others could be hurt emotionally by what he did

In family conferences, when his mother talked about the anguish he had caused, Peter was surprised and called himself the 'victim,' unable to see how he had used his family and friends for his own ends - for psychopaths, other people are always an It, a mark to be duped, used, and discarded

Some argue that the Dark Triad actually describes different points along the same continuum from healthy narcissism to psychopathy, and that the Mach represents the subclinical, nonimprisoned version of the psychopath

The main test for psychopathy includes a measure of 'Machiavellian egocentricity,' such as agreeing with statements like 'I always look out for my own interests before worrying about those of the other guy'

Unlike Machs and narcissists, psychopaths feel virtually no anxiety: they disagree with statements like 'Making a parachute jump would really frighten me' and seem immune to stress, remaining calm in situations that would make many other people panic
In experiments where people wait to receive an electric shock, ordinarily they show high levels of sweating and a quickened heart rate - autonomic indicators of anxiety - but psychopaths do not

A brain imaging study with a group of criminal psychopaths suggests a deficit in circuitry centering on the amygdala, within a brain module essential for reading fear or sadness on people's faces or in their voices, and deficits in the prefrontal area that inhibits impulse

'Successful psychopaths' are those involved in theft, drug dealing, violent crimes, and the like who have never been convicted or arrested for those acts; they react more anxiously to anticipated threats, and that greater apprehension adds caution, making them less likely to end up in prison

Torture of animals is a childhood precursor of psychopathy in adults; other warning signs include bullying and intimidation, picking fights, forcing sex, setting fires, and other crimes against property and people
One jailed serial rapist said of his victims' terror: 'I don't really understand it. I've been frightened myself, and it wasn't unpleasant'

assets.visual_frame_description: Three sorting chutes stand in a theater of villainy - a mirror, a chessboard, and a mask - while a diagnostic chart compares the trio on empathy, anxiety, and self-assessment; cases slide down as film stills from the Ramayana, Star Wars, and Silkwood.
assets.player_mission: Sort the cases - Andre, the European manager, Peter, the business school students, the erotic-reading study, the corporate scandals - into the chute that owns them: narcissist, Mach, or psychopath. Distinguish them by motive (dreams of glory, ends justify the means, other as object), by anxiety profile, and by self-image, and justify each call with the evidence before the next case slides in.
key_concepts: The Machiavellian type stands as a perennial staple of popular entertainment - as old as the demon Ravana in the ancient Indian epic the Ramayana, as contemporary as the evil emperor in the Star Wars saga: the cad, the unfeeling but smooth villain who ruthlessly exploits

Machs, like narcissists, see others in strictly utilitarian terms as an It to manipulate for their own ends, but far more than the other two branches of the Dark Triad, the Mach remains realistic about himself and others
Narcissists' bias is firmly self-serving: they take credit for successes but never blame for failure, even blithely claiming credit for others' work, and see nothing wrong in this

According to one standard test, a narcissist has a grandioose sense of self-importance, harbors obsessive fantasies of unbounded glory, feels rage or intense shame when criticized, expects special favors, and lacks empathy

American college students see themselves as 'better' than two-thirds of their fellows in most endeavors, while Japanese students rate themselves exactly in the middle - unrealistic self-inflation comes more readily in individualistic cultures like the United States than in collective ones

Organizational narcissism makes pumping up grandiosity the operating norm: healthy dissent dies out, the outfit loses the ability to respond nimbly to harsh realities, and those who challenge the self-flattery are typically demoted, upbraided, or fired

In a prescient scene in the 1983 movie Silkwood, a manager at a manufacturing plant retouches photos of welds on fuel rods headed for nuclear reactors, thinking of himself as a good corporate citizen - a warning against the 'Chernobyls of entire corporations'

Psychopaths can be socially smooth, believing that 'even when others are upset with me, I can usually win them over with my charm,' and some criminal psychopaths read self-help books to better learn how to manipulate their targets
Even as children, many psychopaths displayed coldheartedness: budding psychopaths fail to perceive others' emotional pain and so do not apply any inner brakes on their own meanness or cruelty

Because psychopaths feel no anticipatory fears and are virtually oblivious to the threat of punishment, their indifference to the consequences that keep others law-abiding makes them the most likely candidates for prison among the Dark Triad

Looping ordinarily makes people feel within themselves the distress that another person expresses, but psychopaths fail to resonate in this way - their neural wiring deadens them to the range of emotions in the spectrum of suffering

assets.visual_frame_description: A basketball sideline where a giant coach suspends himself from coaching; a supermarket aisle where a blushing culprit faces forgiving onlookers; and a great hall where the final examination is written, with a caption glowing above the desk: 'Include an evaluation for concern - empathy in action.'
assets.player_mission: Hold the line of the social emotions: face John Chaney's remorse after the hard fouls, forgive the mortified culprit at the supermarket display, and stand your ground at the fourteenth-month mirror where self-consciousness begins. Then confront the triad's missing prods - pride without guilt, shame in stunted form, apprehension that never comes - and write the final examination: the test of social intelligence that a well-prepped Mach cannot ace.
key_concepts: In the final minutes of a close playoff-deciding game, Temple University coach John Chaney sent in a six-foot-three, 250-pound giant with orders to commit 'hard fouls,' and one of those fouls sent an opposition player to the hospital with a broken arm, sidelining him for the rest of the season

Chaney then committed a singular act: he suspended himself from coaching, called the injured player and his parents to apologize, offered to pay the hospital bills, and told reporters, 'I feel very contrite' and 'I'm very, very remorseful'

Remorse like Chaney's is the key distinction between the Dark Triad and others who commit reprehensible acts; remorse, shame, embarrassment, guilt, and pride are 'social' or 'moral' emotions that presuppose empathy and act as inner police

Embarrassment is triggered when we violate some social convention, as with the gentleman who gave an unsparing critique of an actress's performance to a man he'd just met at a party, only to learn that the actress was the man's wife
In one study, when someone who knocks over a supermarket display seems mortified, the people nearby feel far more forgiving than when the culprit appears to be indifferent

Neurological patients prone to faux pas and inappropriate self-revelations turn out to have lesions in the orbitofrontal area; some neurologists theorize these patients can no longer detect expressions of disapproval or dismay and so miss how others are reacting to them

The basic emotions of anger, fear, and joy are hardwired into the brain at birth or soon afterward, but social emotions require self-consciousness, a capacity that begins to emerge in the second year of life as a child's orbitofrontal region grows more mature

At around fourteen months babies start recognizing themselves in a mirror; before age two a toddler remains blissfully oblivious to how others might judge her, and embarrassment is typically a child's first social emotion

In 'altruistic anger' one person punishes another's violation of a social norm - such as abusing trust - even when they are not the victim, and this righteous anger seems to activate a reward center in the brain, so enforcing norms gives a satisfying feeling

Shame arises when others become aware of a wrong we have done and more often leads to defensiveness, while guilt stays private, arising as the feeling of remorse, and may spur people to rectify their wrongs; shame anticipates social rejection, guilt may lead to atonement

Narcissists are driven by pride and fear of shame, but they feel little guilt for their self-centered acts; guilt requires empathy, which the Mach's emotionally distant relationships lack, and shame stirs for Machs only in a stunted form

In the psychopath's absence of both guilt and apprehension, potential punishments lose their power to deter - explosively dangerous combined with an utter lack of empathy with another person's distress - so a sound test for social intelligence should identify and exclude the Dark Triad, and one solution is to include an evaluation for concern, empathy in action

assets.visual_frame_description: A party seen through a radar that traces who is reading whom; a cartoon of a monster on the stairs flickering between two frames of reality; a pair of eyes surrounded by adjectives, one of them glowing as the correct read.
assets.player_mission: Scan a party scene, a cartoon, a visit to the in-laws, a dining hall line, and a hospital corridor, and detect the mindsight glitch in each: the joke that needs two frames, the sarcasm that lands as plain speech, the extreme mistaken for the norm, the eyes that are never met. Ring whether the deficit is autism-spectrum, a normal slip, or a distortion like tray gazing, before the scene's verdict is stamped.
key_concepts: Richard Borcherds, winner of the Fields Medal - the equivalent in mathematics of the Nobel Prize - finds having friends over 'just too confusing,' has trouble following the interplay of glances and smiles, and when guests come over often just reads a book or withdraws to his study

When Simon Baron-Cohen, head of the Autism Research Centre at Cambridge, described in great detail the hallmarks of Asperger's syndrome, Borcherds' matter-of-fact response was 'That's me,' and the math prodigy has offered himself up as Exhibit A in Asperger's research

Borcherds scored low on reading people's feelings from their eyes, on empathy, and on intimacy in friendships, but in the very highest tiers on understanding physical causality and on systematizing complex information
That picture - low on empathy, high on systematizing - is the underlying neural pattern in Asperger's, according to years of research by Baron-Cohen and many others

Neuroscientists call the ability to apprehend what seems to be going through someone else's mind 'mindsight' - peering into the mind of a person to sense their feelings and deduce their thoughts, the fundamental ability of empathic accuracy

Without mindsight our relationships would be hollow; we would relate to other people as though they were objects, without feelings or thoughts of their own - the predicament of people with Asperger's syndrome or autism: we would be 'mindblind'

To get the joke in the Mean Monkey cartoon - 'I give up, Robert. What has two horns, one eye, and creeps?' - we must read two minds, the boy's and the father's, and Freud proposed that all jokes juxtapose two different frames on reality

In the treat-hiding test, four-year-olds will say the older child will look in the original hiding place, while three-year-olds guess the new place - four-year-olds have realized that someone else's understanding can be different from their own

In the Mean Monkey puppet game, by around age four children 'get' that the puppet always chooses their preferred sticker and quickly learn to tell him the opposite of what they really want, while younger children innocently continue telling the truth and never get the sticker

Catherine Sanderson, the psychologist who discovered tray gazing at Amherst College, found that each woman saw the others as much thinner, as exercising more, and as more obsessed with their bodies than they were themselves - when in fact there were no objective differences

The distorted tray-gazing assumptions led the women to diet and, for about a third of them, to engage in induced vomiting or purges - a habit that can evolve into a life-threatening eating disorder - and the more erroneous their assumptions, the more extreme their own dieting
Teasing, tricks, lying, and being mean all demand the same sense of the other's inner world, and mindsight stands as a prerequisite for younger children's ability to joke, or to get a joke

credibility.basis: Goleman popularizes social-neuroscience research but overreaches on mirror neurons, 'social intelligence' as a measurable trait, and deterministic brain claims, drawing sharp cr...

assets.topic: Dialogue: The Pause and the Punch Line
assets.visual_frame_description: A Cambridge study with books to the ceiling where a man withdraws with a book; a schoolyard where a girl loops the same phrase word for word; a car on a highway where a mother and daughter discuss the pause in a conversation.
assets.player_mission: Play Borcherds at the party and then the patient guest who explains the punch line and the blushed exit; play Temple Grandin the Tape Recorder on the schoolyard; and play Layne Habib coaching her daughter to wait for the pause - then answer as the daughter with her aha moment. Finish as Marie in the car on the way home, and say out loud the 'marvelous' remark that everyone but the mindblind understands.
key_concepts: For Borcherds, communication is purely functional: he shuns the telephone (though he can explain the physics of how it works), restricts his e-mail to the bare basics of work-related information, and runs from place to place even when someone else has been walking along with him

Temple Grandin was diagnosed as autistic in childhood; the other kids called her Tape Recorder because she used the same phrases over and over again in every conversation, like 'I went to Nantasket Park, and I went on the rotor, and I really like the way it pushed me against the wall'
Adolescence announced itself to Temple Grandin as a 'tidal wave of anxiety that never stopped,' another symptom of autism

Watching cattle calm down in a squeeze chute at her aunt's dude ranch in Arizona, Grandin realized that deep pressure is calming - like a baby in swaddling - and with the help of a high school teacher built a human squeeze chute of wood and an air compressor that she still uses to calm down
Layne Habib's teenage daughter, who has Asperger's syndrome, blurted out 'Oh! You're so old!' on seeing a middle-aged shopkeeper and added matter-of-factly, 'In Japan the elderly are honored'

When Habib told her daughter to wait for a pause rather than saying 'I feel like leaving now' and walking off, the daughter replied, 'I get it now... You fake it. No one could be all that interested in everything a person says. You just have to wait for the pause to come so you can leave'
Habib, who teaches social skills to groups of children with special needs like her daughter, says mastering these rudiments helps them 'join the world, instead of staying isolated in their own'
While members of the Dark Triad may scrutinize social rules in order to manipulate others, those with Asperger's study them just to get along

Marie, who dreaded her husband's boring relatives, answered his question about the visit with 'Oh, marvelous. I could hardly get a word in edgewise' - sarcasm that eludes people with autism, for whom even the simplest social algorithm, like why a snub makes someone feel badly, remains a mystery
To 'get' a sarcastic remark we need to perform a subtle social math, premised on the realization that what the person says is not what the person means
Boys are four times as likely as girls to develop autism and ten times more likely to be diagnosed with Asperger's

Baron-Cohen devised a test called the EQ, for 'empathy quotient' (not for emotional intelligence), on which women on average outscore men, as they do on measures of social cognition and on reading a person's feelings from their eyes alone

credibility.basis: Goleman popularizes social-neuroscience research but overreaches on mirror neurons, 'social intelligence' as a measurable trait, and deterministic brain claims, drawing sharp cr...

assets.visual_frame_description: A developmental psychology lab with a mirror, a jar of crackers and apple slices, and a toy treat hidden under a cup; a wall chart of milestones lights up as each child passes, and an fMRI display shows the fusiform gyrus dark for faces and bright for numbers.
assets.player_mission: Audit children's progress through the mindsight milestones: the eighteen-month mirror mark, the eighteen-month snack preference, the three-versus-four-year-old hiding test, and the Mean Monkey game - and file each child at the correct stage. Then file the imaging findings: the fusiform face area that lights for faces in ordinary brains, for phone directories in autistic ones, and for cardinals in birdwatchers'.
key_concepts: At about eighteen months, place a large mark on a baby's forehead and have her look in a mirror: those younger than eighteen months will touch the mark on the image in the mirror, while those older will touch their own forehead - the younger babies have not yet learned to recognize themselves

In the snack test around eighteen months, after you exhibit clear disgust at the child's choice and a strong preference for the opposite snack, children younger than eighteen months will generally offer the snack they liked, while older ones will offer the snack you preferred

Having mindsight demands these basic skills: distinguishing oneself from others, understanding that someone else can think differently from oneself and perceive situations from another perspective, and realizing that their aims may not be in one's own best interests

As growing children master these social lessons - typically in their fourth year - their empathy approaches that of an adult, part of innocence ends, and they become clear about the difference between what they merely imagine and what actually happens
Mirror neurons may be crucial for mindsight: even among normal children, the ability to imagine another person's perspective and to empathize correlates with mirror neuron activity
fMRI imaging of young teens reveals that, compared to normal children, an autistic group showed a deficiency in prefrontal cortex mirror neuron activity while reading and imitating facial expressions

Brain scans of people with autism have found inactivity in a region known as the 'fusiform gyrus face area' while looking at a person's face; in birdwatchers the fusiform area lights up when a cardinal flies by, and in auto enthusiasts when a BMW drives up

For autistic people the fusiform face area fails to activate even when they look at the faces of their family, but it does activate while they look at whatever happens to fascinate them, such as the numbers in a phone directory

Of the close to two hundred muscles of the face, those surrounding the eyes are particularly fine-tuned to express feelings, yet people with autism avoid looking there and so miss crucial emotional information

Avoidance of eye contact may be one of the earliest indicators that a baby will grow up to become autistic; when autistic infants look at eyes, their amygdala reacts wildly, indicating intense fear, so instead they look at the mouth, which conveys little about someone's inner state

Blind children make up for their inability to see faces by developing a keen sensitivity to the emotional cues in voices, made possible because their auditory cortex takes over their unused visual area - making some, like Ray Charles, superb musicians
A simple rule of thumb has emerged in studies of those with autism: the less activation in the brain's face-reading area while they look at someone, the greater their interpersonal difficulties

assets.visual_frame_description: Twin sorting towers stand side by side - one inscribed with a heart, one with a gear - with a middle track for the balanced brain; faces and machines stream in to be filed while a caption reads 'Systemblind' over the left chute.
assets.player_mission: Sort the cases - Borcherds, Grandin, the math savant, the ultra-empathic psychotherapist, the balanced physician, the 'Where's Waldo?' searcher - into the extreme male brain, the extreme female brain, or the balanced brain. Justify every placement with the scorecard before the next case drops onto the sorting towers.
key_concepts: Simon Baron-Cohen makes the radical proposal that the neural profile of people with autism and Asperger's represents the utter extreme of the prototypical 'male' brain, whose circuitry for empathy remains stunted but which is paired with intellectual strengths

The extreme male brain has no clue when it comes to mindsight but excels at understanding systems - the stock market, software, quantum physics - like savants who can solve complex math problems at rates matched only by computers

The most extreme 'female' brain excels at empathy and understanding others' thoughts and feelings, shining at callings like teaching and counseling, but has grave difficulties with systematizing - it is, in Baron-Cohen's word, 'systemblind'

Men score higher than women, on average, on tests of an intuitive knack for mechanics, keeping track of complicated systems, 'Where's Waldo?' fine attention, detecting figures hidden among complex designs, and visual search in general
On these systemizing tests people with autism outscore most men, just as they score the poorest of any group on tests of empathy
Baron-Cohen would abhor any attempts to use his theory to discourage women from becoming engineers - or men from entering the ranks of psychotherapists, for that matter

For the vast majority of people, men's and women's brains are in the same ability range for empathy and systems thinking, and many women are brilliant in systematizing while many men are superb at empathy
Temple Grandin has published more than three hundred scholarly papers in animal science, and her designs are used by half the cattle-handling systems in the United States
Grandin's remarkable understanding of how to make conditions more humane for cattle made her a leading reformer in the quality of life of the world's agricultural animals

The optimal pattern, says Baron-Cohen, is a 'balanced' brain with strengths in both empathy and systematizing - like the physician who renders precise diagnoses and elegant treatment plans while making patients feel heard, understood, and cared about

Those with the most 'male' brains have a high likelihood of exhibiting symptoms of Asperger's or autism, but they can excel in many fields if, like Professor Borcherds, they find a congenial setting to apply their talents
Yet the ordinary social world seems an alien planet to them, so that the most basic rudiments of interaction have to be learned by rote, if at all

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Eyes Test Gauntlet
assets.visual_frame_description: The long dark tube of an MRI machine with a small video monitor showing a pair of eyes and two buttons; around it the milestones rewind from the Mean Monkey puppet to the mirror mark, and a face grid glows where the eyes meet and the rest of the face fades.
assets.player_mission: Lie inside the fMRI beside Baron-Cohen's subjects and call each pair of eyes - sympathetic or unsympathetic - while the autistic group and the ordinary group are scored against you. Then enter the fusiform darkness: track the gaze that every autistic child avoids, follow the voice that blind children learn to read, and run the milestones backward from Mean Monkey to the eighteen-month mirror to win mindsight for the mindblind.
key_concepts: Baron-Cohen's research team compared people with autism and ordinary people as each lay inside the fMRI while a small video monitor displayed photos of people's eyes; the subjects pushed a button to indicate their choice from two offered feelings such as 'sympathetic' or 'unsympathetic,' and the autistic subjects, as expected, were largely wrong

This simple task revealed which parts of the brain are involved in this small act of mindsight: in addition to the orbitofrontal cortex, the key regions included the superior temporal gyrus and the amygdala

Paradoxically, examining the brains of those who lack finesse offers clues to the layout of the social brain: comparing differences between normal and autistic brain activity highlights the circuitry that underlies a good part of social intelligence itself
Even among normal children, the ability to imagine another person's perspective and to empathize correlates with mirror neuron activity

Later, if someone takes the time to explain to Borcherds the punch line of a joke, or why one guest stalked out in a huff or another blushed with embarrassment, it can make sense to him - but in the moment all this social haze just goes over his head

Most infants show activity in the brain's facial fusiform area when they look at someone's eyes - but autistic children do not, though the area does activate while they look at a cherished object or neat patterns, such as the way they have arranged their favorite videotapes on a shelf

Autistic children show the fusiform activation when they look at whatever happens to fascinate them - the numbers in a phone directory, a neatly arranged shelf - but not when they look at a face, even a family member's

Largely indifferent to human interaction, people with autism make little or no eye contact with anyone, thereby missing out on the building blocks of human bonding as well as empathy; the resulting gap in social learning contributes to their massive failure to sense how another person feels

Because the finest facial muscles are those surrounding the eyes, avoiding the eyes means missing crucial emotional information, and avoidance of eye contact may be one of the earliest indicators that a baby will grow up to become autistic
We are all mindreaders, depending on a continual stream of such snap judgments - mindsight on the run - and a seamless social life depends on it

Those who perform such everyday mindreading more accurately avoid the error of taking the extreme as the norm: they first gauge how similar the other person is to them, and if they sense similarity, they simply assume the other person thinks and feels much as they do
Such neural capacities matter immensely, not just for the richness of our interpersonal life but for the well-being of our children, for our ability to love well, and for our very health

credibility.basis: Goleman popularizes social-neuroscience research but overreaches on mirror neurons, 'social intelligence' as a measurable trait, and deterministic brain claims, drawing sharp cr...

assets.visual_frame_description: A baby laboratory turned diagnostic theater: infants in baby seats face a carousel of novel toys while a scanner ring paints each child's amygdala in red-hot overreaction, and an interlab map of Portland, Albany, and a third city flickers with the same mouse strain behaving differently in each.
assets.player_mission: Scan a parade of four-month-olds facing a stream of novel toys and ring the tell in each: the baby who loves the onslaught of novelty versus the one who cries so hard he shakes in protest. Then switch to Crabbe's mouse laboratories and judge whether each mouse's behavior is the same in Portland and Albany, stamping every scene with its verdict on gene expression before the case file seals itself.
key_concepts: Four-month-olds shown a toy they've never seen, then another twenty seconds later and another after that: some babies love this onslaught of novelty, while others hate it, crying so hard they shake in protest
Babies who hate novelty grow into toddlers wary of strange people and places—'inhibited' in Kagan's term—whose inhibition shows up as shyness once they reach school
Kagan speculates the shyness is due to an inherited neurotransmitter pattern that makes the amygdala more excitable, hyperarousing these kids at startling things and novel events
Crabbe's alcohol-loving mouse strain C57BL/6J, one of a hundred or so inbred strains useful for medical research, chose the 'rodent martini' far more often than did other mouse strains
Every mouse in a given inbred strain is, in effect, a clone of every other such mouse—they share their genes like identical twins

In Crabbe's three-laboratory test at the identical point (April 20, 1998, between 8:30 and 9:00 A.M., with identical Purina feed, age, shipping history, and apparatus), strain BALB/cByJ was very anxious in Portland but quite adventurous in Albany
'If genes were all, you'd expect to find no differences whatever,' Crabbe noted of the lab-to-lab anxiety differences
Crabbe bets that mice can 'read' the emotional state of the person handling them—one research assistant, allergic to mice, wore a respirator while holding them
In gene expression, essentially, a bit of DNA makes RNA, which in turn creates a protein that makes something happen in our biology

Of the thirty thousand or so genes in the human body, some are expressed only during embryonic development then shut off forever, while others turn on and off constantly; some express themselves only in the liver, others only in the brain

The methyl molecule, one of the mechanisms of epigenetics, not only turns genes on or off but also tones down or speeds up their activity, and helps determine where in the brain the more than 100 billion neurons end up
Crabbe's finding stands as a landmark in 'epigenetics,' the study of ways the experiences we undergo change how our genes operate—without altering our DNA sequence an iota

credibility.basis: Goleman popularizes social-neuroscience research but overreaches on mirror neurons, 'social intelligence' as a measurable trait, and deterministic brain claims, drawing sharp cr...

assets.visual_frame_description: The top floor of William James Hall, the tallest tower on the Harvard campus: Kagan's old office overlooks Boston while a grown 'Kagan baby' sits across the desk, his fMRI scan glowing on the wall with a still-overreactive amygdala and a colliculus readout spiking at a picture of a baby's head on a giraffe's body.
assets.player_mission: Take the role of the boy identified as inhibited in infancy who learned to feel his fear and act anyway, and walk him through his small victories—the dentist who won his trust, the pool his sister jumped into, the bad dream he learned to calm alone. Then switch seats and interview Kagan on the top floor of William James Hall: does the amygdala still overreact even when the behavior has changed, and what exactly did the fMRI show in those twenty-two kids?
key_concepts: Kagan has studied the inhibited babies' trait for close to three decades and, by now semiretired, still follows some of the 'Kagan babies' into their early adult years

In an fMRI study of twenty-two Kagan babies, identified as inhibited as children and now in their twenties, their amygdalas still overreacted to anything out of the ordinary just as they had done before

One neurological indicator of the timidity profile appears to be higher activity in the colliculus, a part of the sensory cortex that is activated when the amygdala detects something anomalous and possibly threatening

The colliculus circuitry triggers whenever we perceive a discrepancy, like a picture of a baby's head on a giraffe body—the images need not be outright threats, anything strange-looking or 'crazy' will do the trick
Kids who have low reactivity in these circuits tend to be outgoing and sociable, while highly reactive youngsters shy away from anything unusual; the novel frightens them

Kagan discovered that when parents encourage these timid kids to spend time with peers they might otherwise avoid (sometimes parents have to be forceful), the children can often overcome the genetic predisposition to shyness
After decades of research, among children identified shortly after birth as 'inhibited,' only one-third still showed timid behavior as they entered early adulthood
'Seventy percent grow toward health. Temperament may constrain what can be, but it does not determine it,' Kagan said of the inhibited children

One formerly inhibited boy overcame his fear of shots by finally finding a dentist who won his trust, learned to swim after seeing his sister jump into the pool, and eventually calmed himself after bad dreams—writing, 'Because I now understand my predisposition towards anxiety, I can talk myself out of simple fears'
Kagan's granddaughter, very shy at six, told him: 'Make believe I don't know you—I have to practice not being shy'

Neuroscientists use the term 'neural scaffolding' for how a laid-out brain circuit's connections strengthen with repeated use, explaining why an established behavioral pattern requires effort to change—though new opportunities or effort and awareness can lay down a new track

Kagan's books, with titles like Galen's Prophecy, suggest his fluency with philosophical as well as scientific issues, and his late-1970s claim that inhibition had biological causes ran against an ethos that traced every childhood problem to an error in parenting

credibility.basis: Goleman popularizes social-neuroscience research but overreaches on mirror neurons, 'social intelligence' as a measurable trait, and deterministic brain claims, drawing sharp cr...

assets.visual_frame_description: A genomics ledger bound in lab-coat white where every entry splits into DNA, RNA, and protein columns; a methyl-molecule cursor toggles switches across a wall of gene lights while a balance scale weighs the nurturing mother's lick-and-groom count against the neglectful one's.
assets.player_mission: File every experimental finding under the right entry in the ledger of gene expression: which results demonstrate that possessing a gene is not the same as expressing it, and which show the environment turning genomic on-off switches. For each entry, note the mechanism—methyl, diet, handling, or the mother's licking and grooming—and flag every case that strikes another blow against the naive view of genetic determinism.
key_concepts: Crabbe's now-famous, simple experiment, featured in the prestigious journal Science, showed that minor differences from one laboratory to another—such as how the mice were handled—created disparities in behavior, which implied a difference in how the identical genes acted
Epigenetics shows how our environment, translated into the immediate chemical surround of a given cell, programs our genes in ways that determine just how active they will be
The food we eat contains hundreds of substances that regulate a host of genes, turning them on and off like flickering Christmas tree lights

A bite of broccoli offers a dose of vitamin B6, which spurs the tryptophan hydroxylase gene to produce the amino acid L-tryptophan, which helps synthesize dopamine, a neurotransmitter that stabilizes mood

It is biologically impossible for a gene to operate independently of its environment: genes are designed to be regulated by hormones from the endocrine system and neurotransmitters in the brain, some of which are profoundly influenced by our social interactions
'Social epigenetics is part of the next frontier in genomics,' says Crabbe—'another blow against the naive view of genetic determinism: that our experiences don't matter—that genes are all'

In an adoption natural experiment, children born into families with a history of aggressive, belligerent violence adopted by peaceable families showed just 13 percent displaying antisocial traits as they grew up, versus 45 percent of those adopted into 'bad homes' where aggression had free rein

Michael Meaney of McGill University identified a singular window in development—the first twelve hours after a rodent's birth—during which a crucial methyl process occurs, and how much a mother rat licks and grooms her pups in that window determines how the brain chemicals that respond to stress will be made for the rest of the pup's life

Pups born to the most devoted mothers, who licked and groomed the most, grew up with denser connections between their brain cells, particularly in the hippocampus, the seat of memory and learning, and were especially clever at finding their way around a physical layout
The offspring of less nurturing and inattentive mothers ended up with less dense connections between neurons and scored poorly on solving mazes—the 'IQ test' equivalent for mice

Rat pups completely separated from their mothers while still quite young suffer a crisis that flips off protective genes, leaving them vulnerable to a biochemical chain reaction that floods the brain with toxic stress-triggered molecules, and they grow up easily frightened and startled
The human equivalents of licking and grooming seem to be empathy, attunement, and touch—and how we treat our children will, in turn, set levels of activity in their genes

credibility.basis: Goleman popularizes social-neuroscience research but overreaches on mirror neurons, 'social intelligence' as a measurable trait, and deterministic brain claims, drawing sharp cr...

assets.visual_frame_description: A twin dial scale in a stepfamily living room: nature weighs one pan and nurture the other while 720 pairs of teenagers stream past to be sorted—identical twins, fraternal twins, and every variety of stepsibling—and above them glows the rectangle analogy of the two entangled causes.
assets.player_mission: Sort a stream of evidence—adoption statistics, twin-study percentages, family scenes, and gene-expression patterns—onto the two pans of the nature-nurture scale, then decide when the old distinction itself dissolves. Justify every placement by quoting the finding behind it, and reject any case built on the fallacy that genes and environment are independent of each other.
key_concepts: The century-old debate on nature versus nurture turns out to be pointless, based on the fallacy that our genes and our environment are independent of each other—'it's like arguing over which contributes more to the area of a rectangle, the length or the width'

In the 1980s Plomin startled the scientific world with adopted-twin data asserting a teenager's scholastic ability is about 60 percent due to genes, the sense of self-worth only about 30 percent genetic, and morality but 25 percent

Plomin and others using his method came under scientific fire because they typically assessed impacts only in a limited range of families, mainly twins raised by biological parents compared with those raised by stepparents

The Reiss group at George Washington University—with Mavis Hetherington, an expert on stepfamilies, and Robert Plomin—demanded 720 pairs of teenagers spanning the entire range of genetic closeness in six specific family configurations, with stepparents married at least five years
The Reiss group research found that every child experiences the very same family in sharply idiosyncratic ways—blowing to bits the 'one-family-one-environment school of thought'

Children vie to be unique, which results in their being treated differently, and these unique-to-one-child aspects of family life turned out to have great power in determining a child's temperament above and beyond any genetic influences—making them epigenetic wild cards

A teenager's sense of overall self-worth depends much on how the child has been treated and almost not at all on genetics—and once formed, it shapes her behavior quite apart from the ministrations of parents, the pressures of peers, or any genetic given
A child's genetic givens in turn shape how everyone treats him: parents naturally cuddle with babies who flirt and hug back, while testy or indifferent babies get less cuddling

When a child's genetics lead him to be irritable, aggressive, and difficult, parents tend to respond with harsh discipline, tough talk, and criticism, worsening his difficult side in a vicious spiral that evokes more parental negativity

James Watson—Nobel laureate for the double-helix discovery with Francis Crick—admits to a hair-trigger temper but says he gets over his anger quickly, standing toward the better end of the spectrum of how the anger-inhibiting gene can operate

In the weaker pattern of that aggression gene, the person expresses extra-small amounts of the enzyme that controls aggression, angers easily, stays much angrier, is more prone to violence, and can readily end up in prison

The warmth of parents, how limits are set, or myriad other ways a family operates help set the expression of many genes, but a bossy sibling or screwy buddy both have their impact—the old, clear distinction between genetics and the social world blurs substantially

credibility.basis: Goleman popularizes social-neuroscience research but overreaches on mirror neurons, 'social intelligence' as a measurable trait, and deterministic brain claims, drawing sharp cr...

assets.topic: Boss Battle: Use It or Lose It
assets.visual_frame_description: A snow-covered Nevada schoolyard at dawn where young Milton Erickson's circuitous first track through the snow hardens by day's end into the one fixed route everyone follows; beneath the snow, a cross-section of a growing brain shows circuits pruned like twigs while newborn neurons migrate, each about to make its ten thousand connections.
assets.player_mission: Stand at the crossroads of the sculpting brain and rule on every circuit that streams past: which connections get strengthened, which get pruned like twigs, and which newborn neurons get to wire themselves into the social brain. Forge the neural trail through the snow of experience—attuned peekaboo against the clicking tongue—and decide what gets imprinted before the optimal windows close.
key_concepts: Milton Erickson's tale of the first track through the snow, and the repeated traversing that followed it, offers an apt model for how neural pathways are laid down in the brain: the first connections become strengthened each time the sequence is followed until they become the automatic route
The adage 'use it or lose it' refers to this ruthless neural Darwinism, where brain circuits vie with one another to survive; the neurons lost are 'pruned,' disappearing like twigs cut from a tree

Over the course of childhood and the teen years, the brain selectively loses half those overabundant neurons, keeping the ones that are used and dropping those that are neglected, as the child's life experiences—including relationships—sculpt its brain
The brain and spinal cord contain stem cells that turn into new neurons at the rate of thousands a day; the pace of neuron creation peaks during childhood but continues into old age

A new neuron migrates to its position and over the course of a month develops to make about ten thousand connections, then refines them over the next four months until the pathways are locked in—'cells that fire together wire together'

During that five-or-six-month period, personal experience dictates which neurons the newborn cell will connect with, and Meaney has found that in mice repetitive learning speeds the rate at which new neurons integrate into circuits
Each brain system has an optimal period during which experience maximally shapes its circuitry: sensory systems are largely shaped during early childhood, and language systems mature next
The hippocampus—in humans as in rats, the seat for learning and memory—continues to be strongly shaped by experience throughout life

In humans, the longest window for shaping occurs with the prefrontal cortex, molded anatomically into early adulthood, so the people in a child's life have a decades-long opportunity to imprint that child's executive neural circuitry

Spindle cells—the superrapid connectors of the social brain—migrate largely to the orbitofrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex at around four months and extend connections to thousands of other cells; just where and how richly they connect depends on influences like family stress (for the worse) or a warm and loving atmosphere (for the better)
Richard Davidson: 'There is a lot more plasticity early in life than later... once a circuit is shaped by the environment in childhood, it then becomes quite stable'

In the attuned peekaboo game, the baby at peak excitement abruptly turns away, sucks his thumb, and dully stares into space—a time-out he needs to calm down—while in the unattuned version the mother clicks her tongue and leans into his line of vision, setting him off fussing and grimacing until he turns farther away, sucking feverishly on his thumb
