assets.visual_frame_description: A sorting chamber where study-session gauges flash between focused pleasure and anxiety, a teacher's scorecard shows Tuned In, Upbeat, Positive Regard, and Flexible Rules, and a hippocampus hologram shrinks and swells with each cortisol reading.
assets.player_mission: Sort the students of the national math test into achievers and strugglers by the chemistry of their study sessions - focused pleasure about 40 percent of the time versus great anxiety 55 percent - and grade each teacher by the 910-first-grader study's four winning behaviors. Justify every call with the inverted-U reading on the card before the hippocampus's cortisol count decides the learning outcome.
key_concepts: A group of sixteen-year-olds scored in the top 5 percent on a national test of potential in math, yet some did poorly in their math class despite their aptitude
The high-achieving students experienced focused pleasure about 40 percent of the time they were immersed in their studies - more often than they felt anxious (about 30 percent)
While studying math, the low achievers experienced such optimal states only 16 percent of the time and great anxiety 55 percent of the time

College students taking math exams scored 10 percent better when they were told the test was a practice than when they thought their score could win a cash prize for a team - and under social stress the deficit in working memory was greatest for the smartest students
Almost half a century before, in 1960, Richard Alpert, then at Stanford, showed experimentally what every student already knew: high anxiety cripples test-taking ability
The hippocampus, near the amygdala in the midbrain, is our central organ for learning, converting the contents of working memory held briefly in the prefrontal cortex into long-term storage
The vast majority of neurogenesis - the brain's production of new neurons and laying down of connections - takes place in the hippocampus

Under prolonged stress, cortisol attacks the neurons of the hippocampus; the actual killing off of hippocampal neurons occurs during sustained cortisol floods from severe depression or intense trauma, though with recovery the hippocampus regains neurons and enlarges again

In a simulation, college students who got injections raising their cortisol remembered what they had studied when tested two days later in the mild to moderate range, but at extreme levels the cortisol impaired their recall by inhibiting the hippocampus

New cells take a month to mature and four more to fully link to other neurons, and during this window the environment determines in part the final shape and function of the cell - the more conducive the atmosphere for learning, the better the encoding

The type of stress that most activates the stress hormones lurks in the classroom, in the form of social threats like fears of a teacher's judgment or of seeming 'stupid' in the eyes of other students - and in a chemistry class where a teacher calls students to the board to calculate difficult interactions on the spot, it is a moment of pride for the bright kids and shame for the rest

In a study of 910 first-graders from a national sample, trained observers found the best results when teachers tuned in to the child and responded to his needs, created an upbeat classroom climate, showed warmth and 'positive regard,' and had good classroom management with clear but flexible expectations - while the worst outcomes came from teachers who took an I-It stance and imposed their own agenda; at-risk students with a warm, responsive teacher flourished, learning as well as the other kids, and sixth-graders who had such a teacher earned better grades not only that year but the next as well

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Leadership Contagion Chamber
assets.visual_frame_description: A boardroom where the leader's mood radiates as colored waves washing over rows of seated people, a meter measuring how far each wave moves the team up or past the peak of the inverted U; the door to the toxic boss's office glows red while a report card waits on a desk at the far end.
assets.player_mission: Command the fifty-six simulated teams: calibrate your displeasure to herd your people up the inverted U, never past the tipping point into the zone where panicked efforts produce bad decisions. Then become the secure base - the buffer, the listener, the best friend at work - and finally walk into Pamela's classroom and become Maeva's secure base before the semester's report card is stamped.
key_concepts: Displays of a leader's displeasure make use of emotional contagion: if artfully calibrated, even a burst of pique can stir followers enough to capture their attention and motivate them, and well-titrated doses of irritation - like compliments - can energize

A power dynamic operates in emotional contagion: emotions flow with special strength from the more socially dominant person to the less, because people naturally pay more attention to what the most powerful person says and does
'When my mind is full of anger, other people catch it like the flu,' the head of a small organization told Goleman ruefully

When a manager delivered a piece of bad news with a warm demeanor, people nevertheless rated the interaction positively; when good news was delivered with a sullen expression, the interaction paradoxically left people feeling bad

In a study where fifty-six heads of simulated work teams were moved into good or bad moods, teams with upbeat leaders coordinated their work better and got more done with less effort, while teams with grumpy bosses were thrown out of synch and their panicked efforts to please the leader led to bad decisions and poorly chosen strategies

While a boss's artfully couched displeasure can be an effective goad, fuming is self-defeating as a leadership tactic: relentlessly foul moods corrode the emotional climate, sabotaging the brain's ability to work at its best

People recall negative interactions with a boss with more intensity, in more detail, and more often than they do positive ones - so the ease with which demotivation can be spread makes it imperative for a boss to leave uplifting emotions behind

George Kohlrieser, a psychologist and professor of leadership at the International Institute for Management Development in Switzerland, observes that having a secure base at work is crucial for high performance: feeling secure lets a person focus, achieve goals, and see obstacles as challenges, not threats

Anxious employees readily become preoccupied with the specter of failure, fearing that doing poorly will mean rejection or abandonment, and so they play it safe - while people who feel their boss provides a secure base are freer to explore, take risks, innovate, and take on new challenges

A midlevel executive praised his boss as 'a superb buffer' who absorbed the financial performance pressures from headquarters rather than passing them down, unlike the head of a sister division who subjected employees to quarterly profit-and-loss evaluations for products that take two to three years to come to market

In surveys of more than five million people working in close to five hundred organizations, one of the best predictors of how happy someone felt on their job was agreement with the statement, 'I have a best friend at work'

In a survey of employees at seven hundred companies, the majority said that a caring boss was more important to them than how much they earned, and employees' liking for their boss was a prime driver of both productivity and how long they stayed - while in a New York City middle school, Pamela became Maeva's secure base: she discovered the thirteen-year-old's reading level was that of a kindergartner, and within four months Maeva had passed every class, and students who feel connected to school have lower rates of violence, bullying, vandalism, anxiety, depression, drug use, suicide, truancy, and dropping out

assets.visual_frame_description: A juvenile facility rebuilt as a diagnostic board where every frozen scene is ringed in red while a gauge labeled Neural Imprint swings between Self-Control Circuitry and Hostility Circuitry, and the shadow of a hypervigilant amygdala looms over the prison yard.
assets.player_mission: Scan each institutional scene frozen at its critical moment and name what it teaches the still-plastic neural circuits of the young brain: the dark cell of 'the Hole,' a Missouri team-restraint drill, a circle of check-ins, the jailyard's menace game. Judge whether the setting strengthens the orbitofrontal brake of self-control or hardens an amygdala set for paranoid hypervigilance and a readiness to fight before the verdict is stamped.
key_concepts: Martin, just fifteen, charted his scars on a line drawing of his own body: feet broken at eleven and twelve, hands scarred by fighting and 'stained' by drugs and stolen property, burns from smoking marijuana, and a brain he said had been 'fried' since age eight by pills, weed, meth, alcohol, shrooms, and opium

Missouri's main youth correctional facility was once described by a federal court as having a 'quasi-penal-military' atmosphere and was condemned for banishing unruly inmates to a dark solitary-confinement cell known as 'the Hole'

A former superintendent of that Missouri facility confessed, 'I saw black eyes, battered faces, and broken noses among the boys. The usual corrective procedure among the guards was to knock a boy down with their fists, then kick him in the groin. Many of the men were sadists'

The Missouri network of small homes, established in 1983 in buildings like old schoolhouses and an abandoned convent, houses no more than three dozen teens each and groups them into teams of about ten supervised by two youth specialists

If a Missouri resident acts up there are no isolation cells, restraints, or handcuffs - instead his teammates are taught to grab his arms and legs and hold him until he calms, a technique that has never produced a serious injury, with fights nearly nonexistent
Half a dozen times a day the Missouri teams form a circle to check in about how they feel, and any member may call an extra circle to raise concerns, most often about safety, courtesy, and respect

Survival in the prison yard's I-It universe demands an amygdala set for paranoid hypervigilance, a protective emotional distance or outright distrust, and a readiness to fight - 'we could not design a better environment for fostering criminal instincts'

One neural key to self-control is the array of neurons in the orbitofrontal cortex that can inhibit angry impulses from the amygdala - the circuitry from the OFC to the amygdala forms the brain's brake on destructive urges
People with frontal lobe damage are poor at 'cognitive control': they cannot voluntarily direct their thoughts when swamped with powerful negative feelings, so their cruel impulses go unrestrained

The brain circuit for self-control continues to grow and be shaped into a person's mid-twenties, and the social brain circuits for empathy and emotional regulation are among the last parts of the human brain to gain anatomical maturity

On any given day the United States has more than two million people in prison, or 482 inmates per 100,000 residents - one of the highest rates of incarceration in the world - and the prison population is seven times larger than it was three decades ago

Since only a minority of released prisoners avoid being sent back, the term 'corrections' is a tragic misnomer: nothing gets corrected, and younger prisoners typically become mentored by more seasoned inmates, leaving prison hardened, angry, and more skilled as criminals

assets.visual_frame_description: A town meeting hall lit by low winter light where grown men weep openly and six contrite young men sit facing the community; beside it, a jailhouse phone booth where a former crack addict listens to his mother's silence on the line.
assets.player_mission: Take the mediator's chair in the Bucks County meeting where six young arsonists face the weeping father of the Mood's Covered Bridge, and draw from each boy the emotional aftermath of his act - the sleepless nights, the stomach in knots - before his apology can reach the room. Then switch seats and answer as Emarco Washington on the San Francisco phone, telling your mother you were angry but never wanted to hurt her, and decide whether the words wash over her before the circle closes.
key_concepts: The Mood's Covered Bridge, long a landmark in Bucks County, Pennsylvania, was ravaged by fire early one morning in June 2004, and the six young men arrested two months later were well-known graduates of the local high school, all from 'good' families

At the meeting of townspeople with the six arsonists, one of the boys' fathers admitted he thought about his son's crime constantly, couldn't sleep, and felt his stomach was in knots - and then, overcome, he wept
As they listened to the pain expressed by their family and neighbors, the young men were distraught and contrite; they apologized and said they wished they could undo what they had done
Restorative justice holds that in addition to punishment, criminals should face the emotional aftermath of what they have done and make amends where possible

Mediators in restorative justice programs often arrange for the criminal to repair the specific damage done - whether by making payments, by hearing about the crime from the victim's point of view, or by apologizing with genuine remorse

The manager of a California prison restorative justice program said, 'The victim impact sessions are very emotional. For many men it's the first time they get the connection between their crime and the victim'

Emarco Washington, a teenager addicted to crack who resorted to robbery and assault and who by thirty had served time almost every year since his teens, called his mother on his release from the San Francisco jail and apologized
Washington told his mother it was 'like a rain washing over me' - proof that if he changed his behavior and his language he could show himself and others he wasn't a bad seed
The emotional subtext of restorative justice urges offenders to change their perception of their victims from It to You - to awaken empathy
Brad, sentenced to prison for seriously hurting a classmate in a fight in his college dorm, told Goleman, 'No matter what the charge, basically all the guys are in here because of a bad temper'
In the six-cell special unit Brad was assigned to, prisoners get a daily seminar on telling the difference between actions based on 'creative thinking, stinking thinking, or no thinking'

When a relentlessly taunting cellmate challenged Brad to the prison ritual of a locked-cell fight, Brad refused to fight - 'I've been hit lots of times - I can take it. But I'm not going to fight you' - and the two ended up talking for an hour or two

assets.visual_frame_description: A municipal ledger with three stamped divisions - Prevent, Use Prison Fruitfully, Reintegrate - while case cards fly in from Felton Earls's videotapes of Chicago street life and a wall of brass counters tallies recidivism percentages.
assets.player_mission: Audit the interventions on the Kalamazoo task force's 'what works' list and file each under its turning point: prevention in the neighborhoods, prison time used fruitfully, or reintegration into a web of relationships. Stamp every entry with the hard data that earned it - the Missouri and Maryland recidivism figures, the multisystemic therapy drops, the school program numbers - and flag every institution that is really a college for crime.
key_concepts: Kalamazoo's voters were riled about a referendum to raise $140 million for a new youth prison, and a local judge suggested both sides talk things over at a one-day retreat at the nearby Fetzer Institute

The Fetzer retreat drew church leaders, prisoner advocacy groups, the sheriff, judges, the superintendent of schools, mental health workers, and some of the most liberal Democrats and conservative Republicans
By the end of their day of retreat the Kalamazoo group had found common cause: 'to make Kalamazoo the safest, most just, community in the United States'
The first guiding principle of the Kalamazoo plan is that supportive connections prevent crime - and those connections must start in the neighborhoods where young people most at risk for crime live

A 1999 study found the recidivism rate for the Missouri program was just 8 percent over the three years following a teenager's release, while in Maryland 30 percent of those released from juvenile correctional facilities were back in jail within three years
In the first year after release, Missouri's rate of return to juvenile custody, adult prison, or probation was just 9 percent, compared to 29 percent in Florida
Over four recent years, 110 teenagers committed suicide in juvenile facilities nationwide - while in the twenty years of the Missouri program there have been no suicides

The ten-year study headed by Harvard psychiatrist Felton Earls made videotapes of 1,408 blocks of street life in 196 Chicago neighborhoods and compared them with crime records and interviews with 8,782 neighborhood residents

Earls found two primary influences on a neighborhood's crime rate: its overall level of poverty and the degree of connection among its people, which in tandem outweigh the standard factors of race, ethnic background, or family structure

Even in the poorest neighborhoods, Earls found, positive personal connections were associated with lower crime rates, less drug use among young people, fewer unwanted teen pregnancies, and a rise in children's academic performance

In the mid-1990s a coalition of black ministers took to the stoops and corners of Boston's toughest neighborhoods to bring kids into after-school programs led by local adults, as the murder rate plunged from 151 in 1991 to just 35 ten years later

School-based social and emotional learning programs have reduced fights by 69 percent, bullying by 75 percent, and harassment by 67 percent - and a meta-analysis of more than one hundred such programs showed students' academic achievement test scores ran a hefty 12 percent higher than similar students without the programs

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: College for Crime or Reform School
assets.visual_frame_description: A twin-cell sorting chamber where prison practices slide down chutes labeled Colleges for Crime and Reform Schools in the Deepest Sense, while above them a neural schematic lights up the OFC-amygdala brake and an amygdala glowing red in paranoid vigilance.
assets.player_mission: Drag each practice onto the institution that owns it: the Hole, the menace game, and seasoned-inmate mentoring on the college for crime side; team restraint, check-in circles, and postrelease trackers on the reform school side. Justify every call with the neural evidence - whether the practice builds the amygdala's paranoid hypervigilance or the orbitofrontal brake on destructive urges - before the file cabinet slams shut.
key_concepts: One neural pattern underlying out-of-control violence appears to be an underactivation in the frontal lobes, often due to violent injuries in childhood

The deficits that center on the circuitry running from the OFC to the amygdala - the neural link that forms the brain's brake on destructive urges - are among the most glaring deficiencies in the prison population

From the neural perspective, during imprisonment society has a choice between strengthening prisoners' circuitry for hostility, impulsivity, and violence, or their circuitry for self-control, thinking before acting, and the very ability to obey the law
Perhaps the greatest missed opportunity in the penal system has been the failure to treat younger prisoners who are still within the window where the social brain remains most plastic

A tally of prisoners in state and federal facilities shows that about one quarter are under the age of twenty-five - not too late to nudge the empathy and impulse-regulation circuits into a more law-abiding pattern

An exhaustive analysis of the 272,111 prisoners released from U.S. correctional facilities in 1994 found that over their criminal careers they had been arrested for nearly 4,877,000 crimes - an average of more than seventeen criminal charges each
Two-thirds of those released from American prisons are arrested again within three years

Teens incarcerated for aggressive offenses who go through training programs that teach them to stop and think before reacting, to weigh solutions and consequences, and to stay coolheaded get in fewer fights and are less impulsive and inflexible

The prison population today is seven times larger than three decades ago, and costs have risen from around $9 billion in the 1980s to more than $60 billion by 2005 - the fastest-growing expense for states behind health care

If juvenile prisons were designed as learning environments that enhance the skills people need to stay out of jail - literacy, job training, self-awareness, self-control, and empathy - prison could be a place where neural habits are literally re-formed, 'reform' schools in the deepest sense
Careful evaluation of present-day prison rehabilitation programs has found that those targeting juvenile offenders are among the most successful in preventing a return to crime

Brad's prison world is based on an us-versus-them paranoia in which anyone in a uniform is 'the enemy'; two years after release he was back in college, had moved in with his father, and said of losing his old friends, 'I have no regrets. I'm happy'

assets.visual_frame_description: A young man stands at a fork where one road loops back through familiar corners to a jailhouse door and the other threads through a web of lit homes, classrooms, and church doors; a four-month hourglass pours above while a counter shows recidivism dropping 25 to 70 percent.
assets.player_mission: Walk the perilous four months beside a released young offender as the multisystemic therapy counselor who shadows his life in the home, on the streets, and at school. Search his private world for strengths - the good kid who could be a friend, the uncle who could be a mentor, the church that could offer a virtual family - and steer him away from the old groups while the recidivism counter ticks down from 70 percent toward the golden moment of the first arrest.
key_concepts: Multisystemic therapy has no fifty-minute sessions one on one in a therapist's office - the intervention goes on smack in the midst of life, in the home, on the streets, at school, wherever and with whomever the ex-inmate spends his time

The multisystemic therapy counselor shadows the released offender, gets to know his private world, and searches it for strengths like a good kid who could be a friend, an uncle who could be a mentor, or a church that could offer a virtual family

The multisystemic approach is pragmatic: ratchet up levels of discipline and affection at home, decrease time spent with trouble-prone peers, work harder at school or get a job, and take part in sports
Though it lasts just four months, multisystemic therapy cuts recidivism rates tracked over three years after release by anywhere from 25 to 70 percent
Those recidivism results apply to the most intransigent, difficult prisoners - those whose crimes were violent and serious

The Kalamazoo group identified the perilous moment when a young prisoner returns home as a pivotal turning point, when without intervention it is all too easy to slip back into old groups, old habits, and more often than not jail again
The fastest-growing group in prison are those in middle age, virtually all of them at the inevitable endpoint of a life in crime that began with their first arrest, in their youth

That first arrest is the golden opportunity for intervening, for changing the vector of a young person's life away from criminality - shunting him either into the revolving door of jail or away from it

In the Missouri formula, each teen meets his postrelease coordinator when he arrives at the facility, so by the time he is discharged he has a long-standing relationship with the person who will guide him back into community life
A 'tracker' - typically someone from the teen's hometown or a local college student - monitors his day-to-day progress and helps him find a job

The teens in Missouri's homes live as a 'family' with continuing one-on-one relationships with caring adults, and trust is key: one by one they tell their life stories, tales of domestic violence, sexual victimization, abuse and neglect

One of the Missouri homes is in an abandoned convent and others in old school buildings or large houses, so these teens are not faceless cogs in some vast institution - everyone in each home knows the names of all the residents

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Us-Them Boundary Scanner
assets.visual_frame_description: A rift of darkness runs down a panoramic screen where faces glow on either side - the children of light against the children of darkness - while a scanner overlays the words Us and Them and a gauge shows the gap between attunement and the silencing of empathy.
assets.player_mission: Scan a wall of frozen moments from the apartheid training room to the Columbine commons and name the tell in each: the instant empathy silences, the moment a cognitive category skews into a hostile stereotype, the flash of amygdala-driven anger that flips Us and Them into Us versus Them. Judge whether each scene is closing the divide or widening it before the gulf swallows the frame.
key_concepts: During the last years of apartheid in South Africa, thirty people - half white business executives, half black community organizers - met clandestinely for four days to be trained to conduct leadership seminars together

On the last day the group sat riveted to a television while President F. W. de Klerk gave the now-famous speech that legalized banned organizations and ordered the release of many political prisoners, as Anne Inersebe pictured the face of someone she knew for each organization named

In the ending ritual, a tall, emotionally reserved Afrikaaner stood, looked directly at Anne Inersebe, and said, 'I want you to know that I was raised to think you were an animal' - and with that he broke into tears

As Walter Kaufmann, the translator of Martin Buber, put it, with 'Us-Them' the world is divided in two: the children of light and the children of darkness, the sheep and the goats, the elect and the damned

The relationship between one of Us and one of Them by definition lacks empathy, let alone attunement - the gulf builds with the silencing of empathy, and across that gulf we are free to project onto Them whatever we like

In experiments where volunteers were asked if they would take an electrical shock in place of someone they could not see, the more unlike themselves the other person was described as being, the more unwilling they were to come to the rescue
'Hatred,' said Elie Wiesel, the Nobel Peace Prize winner and Holocaust survivor, 'is a cancer that is passed from one person to another, one people to another'
Northern Irish Protestants and Catholics, like Serbs and Croatians, have battled over the years though genetically they are each other's closest biological brothers and sisters
Groups that are so much alike move from Us to Them via the 'narcissism of minor differences,' seizing on small features that set the groups apart while ignoring their vast human similarities
Prejudice is a hypothesis desperately trying to prove itself to us: once a negative bias begins, we seize on whatever seems to confirm the bias and ignore what does not

Outright anger primes prejudice even in those whose biases are slight - like a match on tinder, antagonism catalyzes the switch from Us and Them, the mere perception of difference, to Us versus Them, active hostility

When flooded by anger and fear, both amygdala-driven, the prefrontal area becomes incapacitated as the low road hijacks the high, sabotaging the ability to think clearly about whether he really has all the bad traits we ascribe to Them

credibility.basis: Goleman popularizes social-neuroscience research but overreaches on mirror neurons, 'social intelligence' as a measurable trait, and deterministic brain claims, drawing sharp cr...

assets.visual_frame_description: A bare South African room where a tall man faces a beaming woman across a circle of chairs, tears breaking his reserve; beside it a grey Belfast parlor where grieving faces soften as an hourglass marking one week drains away.
assets.player_mission: Take the chair of the fifth speaker in that Johannesburg ending ritual and tell Anne Inersebe what you were raised to believe, from the welling of the tears through the silence that follows - then switch seats and receive the words as she does. Afterwards, sit in the Belfast parlor where seventeen bereaved Catholics and Protestants are being coached in forgiveness, and help each mourner stop dwelling on the hurt and honor the murdered family member instead.
key_concepts: The leadership training group in apartheid-era South Africa watched President F. W. de Klerk's speech that heralded the coming end of apartheid, legalized a long list of banned organizations, and ordered the release of many political prisoners

Most participants in the ending ritual said how meaningful the training had been, but the fifth person to speak - a tall, emotionally reserved Afrikaaner - broke into tears after telling Anne that he had been raised to think she was an animal
Kaufmann adds that righteousness, intelligence, integrity, humanity and victory are the prerogatives of Us, while wickedness, stupidity, hypocrisy, and ultimate defeat belong to Them

Once the others are set at a psychological distance they can become a target for hostility - a corruption of categorization, the normal cognitive function the mind depends on to give order and meaning to the world around us
A vague sense of anxiety, a tinge of fear, or mere uneasiness at not knowing the cultural signals of Them can be enough to start the skewing of a cognitive category

As incidents build, apprehension becomes antipathy, and antipathy morphs into antagonism - and if a damning view of Them has already been accepted, the question of whether the stereotype actually fits is no longer asked
For a week psychologists coached seventeen men and women from Northern Ireland, both Catholic and Protestant, on forgiveness - each of them had lost a family member to sectarian violence

During that week the bereaved aired their grievances and were helped to find new ways to think about the tragedy, most resolving not to dwell on their hurt but to honor the memory of their loved ones by dedicating themselves to a more hopeful future
Afterward the Northern Ireland group not only felt less hurt emotionally but also reported a substantial drop in physical symptoms of trauma like poor appetite and sleeplessness

Studies of people posthostility reveal that every time they merely think of the group they hate, their body responds with pent-up anger, flooding with stress hormones that raise blood pressure and impair immune effectiveness
Forgiving someone we've held a grudge against reverses that biological reaction: it lowers blood pressure, heart rate, and levels of stress hormones, and it lessens pain and depression

Especially while wounds are still fresh, forgiveness does not require condoning an offensive act, forgetting what happened, or reconciling with the perpetrator - it means finding a way to free oneself from the claws of obsession about the hurt

assets.topic: Audit: The Implicit Bias Case File
assets.visual_frame_description: A laboratory file room where case cards stream past a reaction-time scanner counting in tenths of seconds, while a wall of portraits - Bill Cosby, Martin Luther King, Jr., Jeffrey Dahmer, Marie Curie - flickers above the cabinets.
assets.player_mission: File every research finding in the prejudice case folder under the mechanism it reveals: the low road's automatic and unconscious stereotypes, the high road's tolerant override, or the emotional valence that Pettigrew says truly predicts hostile action. Stamp each entry with the method that moved the needle - the forty photos, the IQ feedback, the security priming - and note whether the shift survived the twenty-four-hour test.
key_concepts: Us-and-Them comes in many forms, from rabid hatred to unflattering stereotypes so subtle they elude even those who hold them - 'implicit' biases, automatic and unconscious stereotypes that hide in the low road
Such quiet biases seem capable of driving responses like the decision of who to hire from a pool of equally qualified applicants, even when they do not fit our consciously held beliefs

The Implicit Association Test offers a word and asks you to match it to a category as quickly as you can, such as matching 'physics' and 'humanities' to 'women' or 'men' - with the differences counted in mere tenths of seconds and discernible only by computer analysis

Implicit biases skew judgments about people in a target group, from whether to work with someone to judgments of a defendant's guilt; when there are clear rules to follow they have less effect, but the fuzzier the standards, the more powerful they become

A female cognitive scientist was shocked to find that a test of implicitly held biases revealed she unconsciously endorsed a stereotype against women scientists - like herself - so she surrounded her office with photos of famous women scientists like Marie Curie

In a stereotype-reduction experiment, a fifteen-minute session with a carefully selected set of forty photos - widely admired blacks like Bill Cosby and Martin Luther King, Jr., and disliked whites like the serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer - resulted in a dramatic shift: unconscious antiblack attitudes vanished
The positive switch from the photo session was still there when the volunteers were tested twenty-four hours later, and presumably would persist if such images were seen in 'booster' sessions
When people were told that an IQ test showed they had high intelligence, their negative implicit biases vanished - but when they were told the test showed low intelligence, the biases strengthened

Implicit bias against blacks diminished after people were given positive feedback by a black supervisor, and even the explicit resolve to ignore a person's membership in a target group can reduce hidden prejudice

In some neural judo, when people think or talk about their tolerant attitudes, the prefrontal area activates and the amygdala - that seat of implicit prejudice - quiets, so as the high road engages positively, the low road loses its power to stir bias

In Israeli experiments, activating people's sense of security via subtle methods like bringing to mind loved ones shifted prejudiced participants to a positive stance toward groups like Arabs and ultra-Orthodox Jews, making them far more willing to spend time with them

More recent research shows that automatic stereotypes and prejudices are fluid - implicit biases do not reflect a person's 'true' feelings but can shift, a fluidity that may reflect the fact that even the low road remains an eager learner throughout life

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: Contact That Melts the Divide
assets.visual_frame_description: A sorting chamber where pairs of people from across hostile divides slide down chutes labeled Friendships, Casual Contact, and No Contact at All, while a globe above tallies 250,493 respondents in thirty-eight countries.
assets.player_mission: Sort every Us-Them contact onto the scale of what Pettigrew's five hundred fifteen studies actually showed: the emotional involvement that erodes prejudice, the mere casual contact that does little if anything, and the contactless hatred of those arrested for violence in East Germany. Justify each placement with the populations behind the data - the childhood playmates, the Afrikaaner housewives, the Germans with Turkish friends - before the file is sealed.
key_concepts: Thomas Pettigrew, a native of Virginia and one of the first psychologists to plumb the heart of racial hatred, began as a student of Gordon Allport and has led the largest analysis of studies ever on what kinds of contact change hostile groups' views about each other

Pettigrew and his associates tracked down 515 studies dating from the 1940s to 2000 and combined them into a single massive statistical analysis, with responses from an astonishing 250,493 people from thirty-eight countries

The Us-Them divides in those studies ranged from black-white relations in the United States to a multitude of ethnic, racial, and religious animosities around the world, as well as biases against the elderly, disabled, and mentally ill

The strong conclusion of Pettigrew's analysis: emotional involvements like friendships and romances between individuals from either side of a hostile divide make people far more accepting of each other's groups

Having had a childhood playmate from another group typically inoculates people against prejudice later in life - as was found in a study of African-Americans who played with whites as children, though their schools were segregated at the time
The same effect operated under apartheid among rural Afrikaaner housewives who had become friends with their African domestic workers
But mere casual contact on the street or at work does relatively little, if anything, to change hostile stereotypes

Studies that track the time course of across-the-divide friendships show that the closeness itself leads to a reduction in prejudice, and over time the warmth each person feels toward the other generalizes to all of Them
In Europe, people with good friends across tense ethnic divides - Germans with Turks, French with North Africans, British with West Indians - had far less prejudice toward the other group as a whole

'You may still hold a general stereotype about them, but it's not connected to strong negative feelings anymore,' Pettigrew told Goleman - 'the implicit bias may stay, but if my emotions shift, my behavior will, too'

East Germans are on average far more prejudiced against all groups than West Germans, and those arrested for violence against minorities were intensely prejudiced and had virtually no contact with the groups they hated so much

Pettigrew, a Scot whose parents were immigrants, notes that Scots are stereotyped as skinflints but 'we turn that around, saying we're just being thrifty - the stereotype remains, but the emotional valence has changed'

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Villages of New Dawn
assets.visual_frame_description: Two hardscrabble villages on a radio-studio set divided by a field of disputed farmland; above them a loudspeaker broadcasts scapegoating speeches while young listeners huddle over radios, plotting resistance, and the shadow of a hill of bones falls across the land.
assets.player_mission: Work with Ervin Staub and Laurie Anne Pearlman inside the radio soap opera New Dawn, where Rutanagira's faction is goading Batamuliza's village toward an attack on Shema's village over a stretch of fertile land. Rally the young people with friends on both sides, tip off the intended targets, and object openly against the instigators - while the memory of seven hundred thousand slaughtered Tutsis demands you cultivate resistance to hatred before the perpetrators, step by step, exclude their victims from the moral realm.
key_concepts: New Dawn, a weekly radio soap opera popular in Rwanda, is a joint project of Dutch philanthropists and American psychologists whose plot follows tensions simmering between two neighboring hardscrabble villages in dispute over fertile land
From 1990 to 1994, rampaging Hutus slaughtered seven hundred thousand of their Tutsi neighbors, along with moderate Hutus who might oppose the killings

In the Romeo and Juliet twist of the plot, Batamuliza has a romantic interest in Shema, a young man in the other village, while her older brother Rutanagira leads a faction that tries to goad hatred toward the other village to foment an attack - and to force her to marry one of his cronies

Batamuliza belongs to a group with friends in both her own and the other village, who cook up ways to oppose the troublemakers, like tipping off the targets of the planned attack and speaking out against the instigators

'We're giving people an understanding of the influences that led to genocide, and what they can do to see it never repeats,' said Ervin Staub, a psychologist at the University of Massachusetts at Amherst and one of the designers of the show

As a child, Staub was one of tens of thousands of Hungarian Jews saved from the Nazis by Swedish ambassador Raoul Wallenberg, and his book The Roots of Evil summarizes the psychological forces that spawn such mass murder

The groundwork for genocide gets laid during severe social upheavals like economic crises and political chaos, in places with a history of division, when turmoil makes a majority group find appealing the ideologies that scapegoat a weaker group

The hatred spreads all the more readily when the majority group has itself been victimized in the past and still feels wounded or wronged, and violence becomes more likely when targets cannot speak up and bystanders say and do nothing

'If others are passive when you first harm the victims, the perpetrators interpret that silence as an endorsement,' Staub says - 'and once people start the violence, step by step they exclude their victim from the moral realm. Then there's nothing to hold them back'

Staub, working with psychologist Laurie Anne Pearlman, has been teaching these insights and antidotes to hatred like objecting openly to Rwandan groups of politicians, journalists, and community leaders, who apply them to their own experience of what happened
Their research shows that both Hutus and Tutsis who have gone through the training feel less traumatized by what happened to them and are more accepting of the other group

Staub distinguishes forgiveness from reconciliation - the honest review of oppression and efforts at making amends like those of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission in South Africa - and finds Tutsis saying, 'If they apologize, I can see myself forgive'

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Hedonic Treadmill Detector
assets.visual_frame_description: A day clock circles over a superyacht deck where guests eye a Saudi prince's towering neighbor while a scrolling ledger beside them ranks Friends, Relatives, Spouse, Children, Clients, Coworkers, Boss, and Being Alone.
assets.player_mission: Scan a day in the lives of the more than one thousand surveyed American women - the commute, the workday, the evening socializing - and name the happiness source in each frame: the person they are with, or the absence of one. Ring the moment yacht envy starts, when expectations adapt upward on the treadmill that never ends even for billionaires, and flag every scene where a relationship nourishes or merely transacts.
key_concepts: Goleman once met a man invited to spend a week on a private yacht - a 'superyacht' so long it was listed in a special registry of the largest pleasure boats in the world

The guests' thrill turned to envy when an even bigger yacht anchored nearby - among the five largest in the world and belonging to a Saudi prince, with a tender sister ship about the size of their own boat

Daniel Kahneman, the Princeton University psychologist who won a Nobel Prize in economics, dubs such high-end envy the 'hedonic treadmill': as we get more money we adapt our expectations upward and aspire to ever more lofty pleasures
'The rich may experience more pleasure than the poor, but they also require more pleasure to be equally satisfied,' Kahneman says of why the wealthiest people are not the happiest

Kahneman and his research team surveyed more than one thousand American women, asking them to evaluate all their activities during a given day in terms of what they were doing, who they were with, and how they felt
The most powerful influences on how happy the women felt were the people with whom they spent their time - not their income, not job pressures, and not their marital status
The two most pleasurable activities were, to no one's surprise, making love and socializing, while the least enjoyable were the daily commute and work

The ranking of which people primed happiness ran from friends and relatives at the top through spouse or partner, children, clients or customers, coworkers, and boss - with being alone at the very bottom

Emotional contagion means that a goodly number of our moods come to us via the interactions we have with other people, so resonant relationships are like emotional vitamins, sustaining us through tough times and nourishing us daily

Among people around the world, nourishing relationships are the single most universally agreed-upon feature of the good life - all people everywhere deem warm connections with others the core feature of 'optimal human existence'
Kahneman suggests we take stock of the people in our lives and the pleasure we get in being with them, then try to 'optimize' our day by spending more time with them in satisfying ways

Now that neuroscience can put numbers to the raw buzz of fellow feeling, quantifying its benefits, we must pay attention to the biological impact of social life - the hidden links among our relationships, our brain function, and our health

assets.visual_frame_description: A quiet research office where a day grid of activities glows on the wall, each cell linked by threads to faces - friends, relatives, children, coworkers - and a dial marked Well-Being responds to every companion name.
assets.player_mission: Sit across from one of the more than one thousand American women and take her through her day activity by activity - what she was doing, who she was with, how she felt - exactly as Kahneman's interviewers did. Then switch seats and answer as the woman: does the people-ranked ledger of happiness confirm itself in your own words before you decide how to optimize tomorrow's schedule?
key_concepts: Kahneman's research also suggests one way to escape from the hedonic treadmill: a life rich in rewarding relationships
In the day-reconstruction survey, the women who ranked making love and socializing as the most pleasurable activities ranked the daily commute and work as the least enjoyable
Much of what makes life worth living comes down to feelings of well-being - our happiness and sense of fulfillment - and good-quality relationships are one of the strongest sources of such feelings
The marital researcher John Gottman has found that in a happy, stable marriage a couple experiences about five upbeat interactions for every negative one

That five-to-one ratio is perhaps an approximate golden mean for any ongoing connection in our lives; if the ratio were reversed to five negative for every positive interaction, the relationship would be in urgent need of mending
A negative ratio does not necessarily mean we should end relationships - the point is to do what we can to alter the troubling behavior for the better, not banish the person
If others are not willing to change, we can still boost our own resilience and social intelligence, changing our part in the emotional tango
How we impact others speaks to how we fulfill our very responsibilities as caring spouses, relatives, friends, and members of our communities

An I-You approach to others lets empathy proceed to its natural next step, concerned action - the social brain then acts as our built-in guidance system for charity, good works, and compassionate acts
Martin Buber believed that the growing preponderance of I-It relationships in modern societies threatens human well-being, and he warned against the 'thingification' of people
George Herbert Mead, an early twentieth-century American philosopher, originated the idea of the 'social self' - the sense of identity we form as we see ourselves in the mirror of our relationships
Mead proposed as a singular goal for social progress a 'perfected social intelligence,' with greatly heightened rapport and mutual understanding

assets.topic: Audit: The Gross National Happiness Ledger
assets.visual_frame_description: A treasury ledger with two columns - Gross Domestic Product and Gross National Happiness - while a Himalayan flag waves above one page and a debt schedule burdens the other with children's food and medicine.
assets.player_mission: Audit the policies stacked on the world's desks and file each under the measure it truly serves: GDP alone, or gross national happiness. Balance Bhutan's pillars against the accountant's delusion, stamp the compassionate capitalism proposals of Weinberg and Farmer with the human costs they confront, and flag every policy where economic theory stays mindblind to suffering.
key_concepts: The small Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan takes seriously its 'gross national happiness,' which it deems as important as the gross domestic product, and the king declared public policy should be linked to people's sense of well-being, not just to economics
The pillars of national happiness in Bhutan include financial self-reliance, a pristine environment, health care, education preserving local culture, and democracy
A small but growing international group of economists sees as misguided the universal assumption in policy circles worldwide that the consumption of more goods means people feel better off
These economists are developing new ways to measure well-being in terms not just of income and employment but also of satisfaction with personal relationships and a sense of purpose in life

Kahneman noted the well-documented lack of correlation between economic advantages and happiness - apart from a large boost at the very bottom, when people go from being impoverished to being able to make a sparse living

Economists have recently realized that their hyperrational models ignore the low road and emotions in general, and so fail to predict with full precision the choices people will make, let alone what makes them happy

Alvin Weinberg, a longtime director of the Oak Ridge National Laboratory and founder of the Institute for Energy Analysis, coined the term 'technological fix' for tech-engineered interventions in human affairs

Weinberg, now ninety, says 'technology makes it easier and easier to disconnect from other people, and from ourselves' - 'we live in a metaworld, with our focus fixed on the latest technology,' but the issues that matter most are families, community, and social responsibility

Weinberg argues that 'the conventional view holds that capitalism is the only efficient way to allocate resources. But it lacks compassion,' and that a compassionate capitalism that set aside a larger portion of the national budget to good works would be more stable politically

Paul Farmer, the public health crusader legendary for his work in Haiti and Africa, decries the 'structural violence' done by an economic system that keeps so many of the world's poor too sick to escape their plight, and treats health care as a human right

Policies that burden the poorest countries with such huge debts leave them too little to pay for food or medical care for their children - an economic attitude that seems mindblind, lacking the ability to imagine the other's reality

All sectors from schools to hospitals to prisons are vulnerable to the accountant's delusion that social goals can be assessed by fiscal measures alone, which ignores the emotional connections that drive our very ability to be - and work - at our best

assets.visual_frame_description: A twin-scale sorting chamber where encounters land as either I-It or I-You while a banner warns of the thingification of people, and a warm light gathers the scenes of cohousing, caring institutions, and restorative circles.
assets.player_mission: Sort every human encounter onto one of Buber's two sides: the I-It that treats people as things and uses social skills for purely selfish ends, versus the I-You that empathizes and cares. Justify each call - the propaganda lab reading fMRI responses, the fanny-pack psychiatrist-on-call, the cohousing kitchen, the emotional secondhand smoke - before the matrix resolves into the two roads open to this century.
key_concepts: An Orwellian use of social neuroscience findings could be their misapplication in advertising or propaganda, with fMRI readings of a target group's response used to fine-tune and amplify a message's emotional impact

Social neuroscientists are already planning benign applications, like using the discovery of an algorithm for empathy - that physiological match during moments of rapport - to train medical residents and psychotherapists to empathize better with patients

Another planned application is an ingenious fanny pack with physiology-monitoring wireless technology that patients could wear at home twenty-four hours a day, automatically sending a signal when it recognizes the onset of an episode of depression - a virtual psychiatrist-on-call
Given the nourishment offered by wholesome connection, the ways we treat the sick, the elderly, and the imprisoned must be reconsidered

For the elderly, often tucked away in bleak and solitary arrangements, Goleman suggests 'cohousing' - residences where people of all ages live together and share many meals, re-creating the extended family that harbored the aged through most of human history
We can refocus the corrections system to affirm decent connections for prisoners rather than cutting them off from the very human ties that could help set them straight

Leaders themselves set much of the emotional tone that flows through the halls of their organizations, with consequences for whether the outcome is measured in achievement test scores, sales goals, or retention of nurses
As Edward Thorndike proposed in 1920, we need to nurture social wisdom - the qualities that allow the people we connect with to flourish
Strong distressing states like disgust, contempt, and explosive anger are the emotional equivalent of secondhand smoke that quietly damages the lungs of others who breathe it in
Just as we catch a virus from someone else, we may also 'catch' an emotional funk that makes us more vulnerable to that same virus or otherwise undermines our well-being
The interpersonal equivalent of health-boosting would be adding positive emotions to our surroundings - social responsibility begins when we act in ways that help create optimal states in others

Buber's message warns against an outlook indifferent to how others suffer and commends the stance that empathizes and cares - a nurturing outlook that takes responsibility for others as well as for oneself

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Circle of Us
assets.visual_frame_description: A vast map of the twentieth century where a glowing circle labeled Us expands into territories marked Them, fed by threads of light from Whitman's 'breathing, laughing flesh,' while Auden's words burn above a dark horizon and a heartbeat counter measures every connection.
assets.player_mission: Stand on the line W. H. Auden drew - 'We must love one another or die' - and push the boundaries of the circle outward, one relationship at a time, while the raw buzz of fellow feeling you kindle is weighed against the toxic encounters that corrode. Nourish your social connections through a century that tested collective empathy to its limits, and prove that the social brain's wiring connects us all at our common human core.
key_concepts: Walt Whitman's exuberant anthem 'I Sing the Body Electric' proclaims, 'I have perceiv'd that to be with those I like is enough... I do not ask any more delight, I swim in it as in a sea'
Vitality arises from sheer human contact, especially from loving connections - the people we care about most are an elixir of sorts, an ever-renewing source of energy
The neural exchange between a parent and child, a grandparent and a toddler, between lovers or a satisfied couple, or among good friends has palpable virtues
In accord with Whitman, one scientist who studies the survival value of sociability says the practical lesson for us all comes down to 'Nourish your social connections'

Through most of human history the bitter antagonisms that stoked hatred between groups were manageable in a strictly logistical sense, because limited means of destruction kept the damage relatively small

In the twentieth century, technology and organizational efficiency made the destructive potential of such hatred immensely greater, as the poet W. H. Auden so pungently prophesied: 'We must love one another or die'
The crucial challenge for this century will be to expand the circle of those we count among Us, and shrink the numbers we count as Them
We need not accept the divisions that hatred breeds - instead we should extend our empathy to understand one another despite our differences and to bridge those divides
The social brain's wiring connects us all at our common human core
The last century highlighted what divides us, confronting us with the limits to our collective empathy and compassion

We must reconsider the pat assumption that we are immune to toxic social encounters - save for the passing stormy mood, we suppose our interactions matter little to us at any biological level, but this turns out to be a comforting illusion
The new science of social intelligence offers us tools that can push the boundaries of Us outward, step by step
